The algorithm combines localized estimation with a stochastic convex bandit routine applied to the negative logarithm of expected profit. Finally, we complement this result by showing a separation between MHR and regular distributions, proving that the minimax regret rate in the latter setting is $\tilde \Theta(T^{\frac 35})$. This last result contrasts with the $\tilde{O}(\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that can be obtained for one-sided pricing with regular distributions.

title: Patch Attention Wisely: Understanding Patch Length in Attention-Based Forecasting
abstract: Attention-based time series forecasters commonly group consecutive observations into patches. Patch length is known to have a substantial impact on forecasting performance, yet its selection remains largely empirical. We develop a theoretical framework that explains why patch length matters for forecasting accuracy and provides a principled basis for its selection. For linear state-space models, we derive an exact factorization of the forecasting coefficient matrix that separates forecast dynamics from filtering dynamics. We show that dominance of a single forecast component at long horizons does not generally imply a rank-one representation. This explains why longer horizons alone need not reduce representational complexity. We combine the factorization with estimation bounds to develop a patch-selection criterion that balances representation and estimation errors under temporal dependence. Our analysis establishes conditions under which balanced patching is justified and clarifies how predictive structure, head count, training sample size, and long-run dependence enter the selection criterion.

title: Bounded GARCH Processes
abstract: We propose a novel class of Bounded GARCH (B-GARCH) processes designed to characterise the conditional heteroskedasticity of continuous time series constrained within a compact interval. While standard GARCH specifications are tailored for R-valued data, many empirical series, such as realised correlation, unemployment rates, expenditure shares, and relative humidity, are bounded. Fitting a traditional GARCH model to such data creates a severe support mismatch, frequently generating predictions and density forecasts that breach the natural boundaries of the data (boundary violation). Furthermore, conventional approaches utilising non-linear link transformations onto the real line might induce interpretability issues and estimation biases. To address these limitations, our proposed B-GARCH framework ensures a proper predictive distribution and an equation for the dynamic conditional variance with a parameter constraint that strictly preserves the bounded support of the entire process almost surely. We establish the fundamental probabilistic properties of the process, proving strict stationarity and ergodicity, and address parameter estimation via conditional maximum likelihood. The asymptotic consistency and normality of the estimators are rigorously derived, and their finite-sample performance is validated through Monte Carlo simulations. An empirical application to the monthly realised correlation between the Vanguard Real Estate ETF (VNQ) and the iShares 20+ Year Treasury Bond ETF (TLT) demonstrates that B-GARCH models effectively capture volatility clustering while completely eliminating boundary violation issue that plagues traditional GARCH models.

title: Between Hi-Fi and MMI: the overlap of redundancy and synergy in partial information decomposition
abstract: Partial information decomposition (PID) splits the information that two sources carry about a target into redundant, unique and synergistic parts, with nonnegative decompositions lying on a segment where redundancy measures are bounded by the positive part of the co-information and the smaller source-target information. We parameterize this segment by the overlap, the common excess of redundancy and synergy over their net balance, and show that for many of the named PID measures, their redundancy can be written as the largest positive part of the co-information over a set of reference distributions. This common form induces an ordering of those PIDs on the segment. With the smallest redundancy and synergy and the largest unique atoms of any nonnegative PID, the information-theoretic version of Hi-Fi, a feature-importance method, is the zero-overlap end of the segment for two sources, with the maximum overlap bound given by the minimum mutual information (MMI) PID. We introduce, by splitting the co-information into a pairwise maximum- entropy part and the third-order connected information, a PID that sits at zero overlap except when pairwise redundancy and triadic synergy coexist. For three or more sources the bivariate results hold on every pair of merged source groups, and among all nonnegative solutions of the lattice equations MMI and Hi-Fi still give the smallest and largest unique atoms but zero overlap on all pairs at once is often unattainable. Two inequalities across pairs are necessary in general and sufficient for three sources. For identity targets zero overlap is possible exactly when the sources' information diagram is nonnegative. In random three- and four-source distributions zero overlap on all pairs fails in 21-100% of the cases.

title: Doubly-robust causal inference for multi-valued treatment regimes with recurrent neural networks
abstract: We propose a doubly-robust method to estimate the causal effects of multi-valued treatment regimes on patient outcomes. A multi-valued treatment regime assigns personalized treatments from a set of competing options based on a patient's history. Existing methods for optimal treatment regimes are largely limited to binary or continuous treatments. We extend the longitudinal targeted minimum loss-based estimator (LTMLE) to accommodate multi-valued treatments by modeling treatment assignments with a multinomial model. We further integrate recurrent neural networks (RNNs) into the LTMLE framework as learners for the outcome, treatment, and censoring models, and compare this approach to ensemble machine learning. Simulation studies show that LTMLE with either ensemble machine learning or RNNs is approximately unbiased, with close to nominal coverage, whereas sequential g-computation with ensemble machine learning is substantially biased under a dynamic rule. A multinomial treatment model performs similarly to a series of binomial regressions with ensemble machine learning, but yields more stable inference when the treatment model is an RNN.

title: Intensity-Based Estimation of Extreme Value Models for Highly Censored Data via a Latent Poisson Process
authors: Antonio Carlos Pedroso de Lima and L\'igia Henriques-Rodrigues
abstract: Extreme value theory provides a natural framework for modelling rare events and extrapolating tail probabilities, but its direct application to survival analysis is complicated by right censoring, heterogeneous follow-up, and the need for coherent inference beyond the range of the observed data. We propose a Bayesian survival model that integrates extreme value theory with a hazard-based formulation built upon the extended generalized Pareto distribution. Rather than separating the bulk and tail of the distribution through an explicit threshold, the proposed model represents the entire hazard function within a unified parametric framework, allowing moderate and extreme survival times to be analysed simultaneously while preserving the asymptotic tail behaviour implied by extreme value theory. Inference is performed through a two-stage procedure. We further develop bias-correction procedures based on latent representative locations and adaptive partition refinement, and establish theoretical results showing the asymptotic consistency of the proposed approximation under standard regularity conditions. Simulation studies demonstrate that the methodology provides reliable uncertainty quantification across a wide range of tail regimes, censoring proportions, and sample sizes, while remaining robust under moderate model misspecification. The practical performance of the approach is illustrated through an analysis of a heart failure cohort, where the proposed model enables inference on long-term survival probabilities and tail behaviour beyond the observed follow-up period. The resulting framework offers a computationally feasible and theoretically grounded alternative for modelling censored survival data when inference on extreme survival times is of primary scientific interest.

title: Economies of scale and the equity-efficiency trade-off: Evidence from a piped water network in rural Bangladesh
authors: Md. Ahasan Habib and Anna Tompsett
abstract: Policymakers who set prices for public infrastructure often anticipate an equity-efficiency trade-off: while higher prices could increase revenues from fee-paying users, helping to offset costs, they may reduce take-up among the poor. But this trade-off is fundamentally altered in the presence of economies of scale, which are common in infrastructure networks. We elicit willingness to pay for a household-level piped drinking water connection in rural Bangladesh, where truthful revelation of preferences is incentivized by the opportunity to connect to a new pipeline network that we construct, and we use project cost data to measure economies of scale. Combining the two, we show that the cost-effectiveness-maximizing price---that which minimizes the cost per connected household---is zero. Economies of scale strongly dominate revenues raised by user fees. More generally, the two conditions needed for a zero price to maximize cost-effectiveness are important economies of scale and high sensitivity of demand to prices near zero, which is well documented across developing countries. Since a zero price naturally maximizes equity, we conclude that economies of scale can eliminate the equity-efficiency trade-off.

title: Joint Modeling of Conditional Mean and Variability in Multilevel Functional Data: Application to Postprandial Glucose Trajectories in the AEGIS Study
abstract: Functional data analysis provides a framework for studying time-varying associations between covariates and high-frequency biological signals. In digital health, participants often contribute repeated functional trajectories, yet existing multilevel regression methods largely focus on the conditional mean, overlooking variability and its role in biological heterogeneity. We propose a heteroskedastic functional mixed-effects regression framework that jointly models the conditional mean and variance of repeated trajectories, with participant-specific random effects in both components. We also develop a participant-level bootstrap to quantify uncertainty in estimated functional parameters. We apply the method to postprandial glucose trajectories from the AEGIS study. Premeal glucose, carbohydrate intake, and meal type show distinct time-dependent associations with glucose variability, whereas HbA1c is more strongly associated with the conditional mean than with variability. Substantial between-participant differences in residual variability remain even after accounting for observed covariates. These findings show that modeling conditional variability alongside the mean provides insights into glucose regulation and individual heterogeneity that mean-focused analyses may miss. More broadly, the proposed framework enables joint characterization of average responses, variability, and participant-specific heterogeneity in repeated biological signals.

title: Generalized confidence intervals for the covariate-specific overlap coefficient
abstract: Continuous diagnostic tests are often used to discriminate between diseased and healthy populations. Therefore, it is important to look for measures to assess the effectiveness of diagnostic markers in discriminating between these two states. The overlap coefficient (OVL), which is defined as the area of intersection of the graphs of two probability density functions, is considered as a summary measure of diagnostic accuracy. Often additional information is available on some of the covariates which are known to influence the accuracy of such measures. Consequently, in this work we incorporate covariate information using linear regression models with normally distributed errors, enabling the construction of the OVL estimator based on the ordinary least squares estimates of the regression coefficients. We further develop a method for constructing generalized confidence intervals for the covariate-specific overlap coefficient. A simulation study is conducted to assess the finite-sample performance of the proposed generalized confidence interval method and to compare it with other procedures. Finally, an illustration to assess the age-specific accuracy of glucose as a biomarker of diabetes is provided.

title: CountScan: Simultaneous Lower Bounds on Historical Watermark Matches over All Text Intervals
abstract: A provider holding a watermark key may audit an external document and choose passages after reading it. A bound computed for a fixed passage is not valid for a passage chosen after seeing the evidence. One remedy splits the evidence between selection and validation. We take the other route and make the statement hold for every interval at once. CountScan gives finite-sample lower bounds on the number of retained historical watermark matches, simultaneously over all text intervals and count thresholds. Its validity rests on one condition: given the auditor's information, the pivots of positions that are not history matches are conditionally super-uniform. This condition holds when generation uses the key only through the Gumbel-max rule and editors have no access to the key, so the guarantee covers edits that depend on the generated text when the calibrators are nonincreasing. Simultaneity raises the threshold by the logarithm of the document length; for a long interval this costs about that logarithm divided by the critical evidence value, in certified tokens. We give a finite-length expansion of the certified proportion, finite-sample rates for two-level rules with lower bounds of the same order within a pivot-only class, and an upper bound over a calibrator class. On pre-registered holdouts with OPT and Qwen base models at temperature one, CountScan certifies substantial counts; under heavy random edits it remains valid but loses most of its power.

title: MSR-CP: A Modified Segmented Regression Approach to Change Point Estimation in Rainfall Patterns in West Bengal
abstract: This study presents a methodology for detecting change point in precipitation series using a smooth version of segmented regression model. We examine several existing change point detection methods and identify their limitations in capturing gradual changes commonly observed in climate data. To address these limitations, we discuss an extension of the traditional segmented regression model enabling the detection of gradual shifts in trend. The developed methodology is further extended to accommodate dependent error structures, which are common in time series data. Extensive simulation studies are conducted to evaluate the performance and computational efficiency of the proposed approach relative to existing methods. The methodology is subsequently applied to 60 years of monsoon rainfall data from two districts of West Bengal, India. This approach offers improved insights into evolving rainfall patterns and serves as a useful tool for climate data analysis and long-term forecasting.

title: Discrete Choice under Congestion: Equilibrium and Welfare
abstract: In many choice settings, a rise in aggregate demand for an option lowers an individual's payoff from choosing it. Driving becomes less attractive than taking a train when more commuters drive, clogging the highway. In such cases, a targeted intervention that mitigates the externality at the congested option can divert it elsewhere and also undermine preference based sorting, making overall welfare effects theoretically ambiguous. We develop an empirical framework to analyze such scenarios of endogenous congestion. We show that in these settings, equilibrium exists and is unique without restrictions on functional-form of utilities or dimension/distribution of preference heterogeneity, and even when congestion at one option affects payoffs from other choices. Under a linear-index structure, micro-data on choice enables semiparametric identification of utility contrasts and welfare effects of some, but not all, interventions. We apply the framework to Cambridge undergraduate admissions, where candidates apply through one constituent college, and admission probability depends on application numbers relative to capacity in that college. Using administrative micro-data on 25,325 applicants, we calculate welfare under two counterfactuals: (i) centralized random allocation and (ii) higher rent at popular colleges. Random allocation reduces welfare for everyone: it removes individual choice without improving admission chances since, by design, lower congestion at a college exactly counterbalances the lower probability of being allocated there. Targeted rent increase produces both gains and losses, with median loss for men and median gain for women. This exercise shows how identified preferences and equilibrium feedback jointly determine welfare when choices entail externalities.

title: Unobserved Consideration and Consumer Welfare
authors: Debopam Bhattacharya and Ryan J. Martin
abstract: Can welfare effects of price change be identified when consumers' consideration sets are heterogeneous and unobserved? We establish that the welfare distribution is the same functional of structural choice probabilities under stable but limited consideration as under full consideration. The result permits unrestricted income-effects, preference heterogeneity, and dependence between preferences and consideration. Within this class, limited consideration admits a full-consideration representation preserving choice-probabilities and money-metric compensation: consideration/preferences can remain unidentified while demand and welfare are identified. When consideration sets contract as prices rise, the welfare distribution can be bounded using demand and a bound on choice-set attrition.

title: Designing Public Information for Strategic Advice
abstract: A principal chooses an action using advice from an expert who privately knows local conditions. Before receiving advice, she can commission a public study of an independent state, such as future demand, that changes the expected conflict between their preferred actions. We show that the communication protocol determines the optimal study. Under optimal mediation, the value of advice is convex in conflict, making full revelation optimal. Under commitment to an action rule, the principal may prefer no information, while informative optimal studies include a report certifying high conflict. Under unmediated cheap talk, changes in the number of equilibrium messages create upward kinks in the value of advice. Optimal studies avoid interior communication thresholds and can induce two distant communication regimes while skipping every regime in between, strictly outperforming both full revelation and no information. When the principal retains the raw data, selective public disclosure can improve advice without sacrificing forecasting precision. We discuss implications for fiscal forecasts and spending agencies.

title: Distributed Optimization Involving Non-Lipschitzian, Linear Composite Functions: Unified Algorithm Design and Convergence Analysis
abstract: This paper formulates a generic distributed nonsmooth optimization problem subject to edge-based equality constraints, local inequality constraints characterized by general convex functions, as well as globally coupling constraints including affine equality and nonlinear inequality. The terminal goal is to minimize the sum of local non-differentiable convex functions and proximable nonsmooth convex composite terms attached to linear operators, over networked multi-agent systems. This formulated framework not only applies in complex practical problems but also reduces to existing distributed optimization structures. To cope with technical issues caused by local linear mappings, potential multiple nonsmooth functions and coupling nonlinear constraints, we first derive a new local first-order condition, and further present a novel fully distributed optimization algorithm based on variable decompositions and proximal operators. Specifically, the proposed algorithm allows each agent to update states via local information exchange and through {locally fixed step-sizes}, and to find inexact solutions of subproblems without loss of convergence speed. In contrast to existing tailor-made algorithms for the bounded gradients of objective functions or affine constraints, our algorithm is capable of solving more practical cases involving general convex functions and nonlinear constraints. Under mild assumptions, the convergence rate $o(1/k)$ in terms of the optimality and successive-difference metrics is achieved, by constructing the equivalent variational inequalities of the proposed algorithm. Finally, numerical experiments on practical application problems illustrate the theoretical results.

title: Stay, Reposition, or Recharge: Battery-Aware Operation of Robotaxi Fleets
abstract: Electric robotaxis are rapidly expanding from pilots to scaled commercial deployment; unlike traditional human-driven ride-hailing vehicles, they require centralized fleet control and careful management of vehicle state of charge (SoC). We study how a fleet manager should jointly make service, empty repositioning, idling, and charging decisions in such systems. We develop a continuous-time fluid model in which vehicles evolve across location-charge states, and identify two forms of charge-aware control that are absent from classic repositioning models: early return-to-depot (RTD) and charge-aware repositioning. In particular, the optimal solution admits simple threshold structures. Each location has a battery threshold such that vehicles should return to the depot to recharge when their SoC is below it and should not do so when their SoC is above it. Vehicles should not reposition below the same threshold either; above it, the choice of destination depends on whether a vehicle's SoC matches the destination's battery sensitivity, a notion we introduce in the paper. We then quantify the value of charge awareness by comparing fully charge-aware policies with charge-oblivious policies that ignore SoC in RTD and repositioning decisions. We show that the performance gap can be unbounded, driven by a dilemma between under-utilizing high-charge vehicles and over-sending low-charge vehicles to locations from which charging is costly. A numerical case study calibrated using 2025 NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission trip records illustrates these thresholds and shows that charge-aware control can generate substantial gains in a realistic urban network. Importantly, simple threshold-based heuristics recover most of the value of the fully charge-aware solution.

title: Willingness-to-pay space and preference space: a unified treatment of equivalence, heterogeneity and interpretation
abstract: A growing number of choice modelling studies estimate their models "in willingness-to-pay (WTP) space", yet often treat this as a different model that fits better (or worse) than "preference space", and misread what its parameters represent. This note brings together and makes precise insights that have mostly been stated only in scattered places, organising them around a single condition for two specifications to be the same model. WTP space is a reparameterisation, and with non-random coefficients the two spaces give identical likelihoods, WTP estimates and standard errors. With deterministic heterogeneity in cost sensitivity, or non-linearity, WTP must still be computed as a ratio of partial derivatives, although a simple normalisation recovers a directly estimated WTP at a reference point. With random heterogeneity, latent class models are equivalent in the two spaces, while other mixtures are equivalent only when the implied distributions match, as with full-covariance lognormals, and independence is not a neutral assumption.

title: Bayesian Spatio-temporal Modeling of Multi-Site Wastewater Surveillance Data
abstract: Wastewater surveillance provides population-level evidence of infectious disease activity. As surveillance expands across multiple sites, repeated measurements must be analyzed jointly while accounting for differences among sites and the public health regions they represent. We develop a Bayesian spatio-temporal framework that decomposes wastewater measurements into a shared epidemic curve, spatially correlated regional deviations, persistent site effects, and within-site temporal dependence. This hierarchical decomposition accommodates unequal observation windows and sampling schedules, allowing regional trajectories to be compared while preserving site-level heterogeneity. A direct marginal spatial covariance specification further separates the magnitude of regional variation from the strength of association between neighboring regions, providing distinct interpretations of these two sources of spatial variation. We also introduce region-specific time shifts to distinguish regional leads and lags in epidemic timing from differences in signal levels and local fluctuations. Simulation studies demonstrate the recovery of these components and show that omitting true time shifts can lead to increased estimates of residual temporal variation. Application to Ontario SARS-CoV-2 wastewater surveillance data reveals persistent site heterogeneity, within-site temporal dependence, and spatial association among neighboring regions. Regional timing differences are more pronounced during the first year of Omicron than in the XBB-and-later period.

title: Learning and Steering in Incomplete-Information Games
abstract: In many modern multi-agent systems, a mediator seeks to influence strategic decision dynamics using only outcome-level feedback and without knowing agents' utilities. In this work, we study how a mediator can learn an unknown game and steer adaptive agents toward outcomes that maximize her utility using only trajectory feedback. The mediator knows the game form and her own objective, but not the agents' utilities. Moreover, she commits to nonnegative payments and provides recommendations and contexts, but receives only a single realized terminal outcome rather than full-information feedback. We develop halving-type algorithms that learn utility differences in normal-form games and conditional continuation-value differences in extensive-form games, achieving a sample complexity of $\widetilde O(\varepsilon^{-2})$ that matches worst-case lower bounds up to logarithmic factors. We then combine these learning procedures with a Lagrangian formulation in an online Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm that interleaves learning, equilibrium computation, and steering toward mediator-optimal extensive-form correlated equilibria (EFCE). With high probability, the Learn-Compute-Steer algorithm achieves a directness gap and an optimality gap of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/4})$, while time-average payments are of $\widetilde O(T^{-1/8})$.

title: Cores of $3$-distant convex games
abstract: Convex cooperative games have a nonempty core and admit an efficient construction of core allocations. However, economically natural local frictions may violate convexity. We study the core of $3$-distant convex games, which permit violations of convexity only between closely related coalitions. Although the core of such a game may be empty, we establish a simple necessary and sufficient condition for its nonemptiness. We also develop a strongly polynomial-time combinatorial algorithm for finding a core allocation whenever one exists. Finally, we demonstrate the applicability of the framework to oligopolistic competition with merger synergies and profit allocation of joint production with complementary inputs.

title: Identification and Bounding of Joint Expectation over Potential Outcomes
abstract: The joint expectation of functions of potential outcomes $(Y_1,Y_0)$ is a fundamental quantity in causal inference, particularly when investigating the variation or heterogeneity of causal effects. This paper provides novel assumptions for their identification: comonotonicity and countercomonotonicity. These assumptions offer a unified framework for their identification across discrete, continuous, and mixed outcome variables. In the absence of these assumptions, we derive sharp bounds for two broad classes of functions, yielding new results for bounding moments of individual causal effects, which are central to measuring effect heterogeneity. We present corresponding estimation methods and illustrate them in simulation studies and real-world datasets.

title: Adaptive Experimentation Can Hide Model Error:Detection Limits and Falsification Budget
abstract: An experiment can be informative about the parameters of a working model and uninformative about whether that model is wrong. Adaptive design can reinforce this mismatch by repeatedly selecting settings where an incorrect model fits. We bound the power of any valid adequacy test in terms of the experimenter's own sampling distribution, then distinguish information absent from the selected data from information lost by the detector. A computable diagnostic measures unresolved error relative to a declared expansion of the working model. It motivates a training-free rule that reserves part of the design budget for falsification. The empirical record is mixed: the independently specified primary study fails detection eligibility, and a later numerator diagnostic fails its improvement criteria. After the frozen rule fails on fresh continuous-null panels, a disclosed secondary horizon-calibrated revision detects 35.8% of misspecified campaigns versus 31.7% for a class-separation control at T = 240, but has no resolved advantage at T = 480. In a corrected 289-unit measured replay it improves on random design and trails class-discrimination EIG. A conditional futility bound explains why remaining time matters without proving the gate constant or its power. These results support separating parameter learning, model checking and detector performance; they do not establish a universally superior design policy or prospective scientific discovery.

title: marp: Model-Averaged Inference for Parametric Renewal Processes in R
abstract: Renewal processes model inter-event times between recurrent events using a parametric distribution, but selecting a single model can ignore model uncertainty and affect inference, particularly in small samples. This paper introduces marp, an R package for model-averaged inference in parametric renewal processes. The package fits six commonly used distributions, compares them using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria, and reports selected-model and model-averaged estimates of the mean inter-event time, event probability and hazard function, with percentile and Studentised bootstrap confidence intervals. A simulation study under three data-generating models showed that model averaging did not improve point estimation but often improved interval coverage relative to the AIC-selected model. Applications to seizure-recurrence and engineering failure-time data illustrate the proposed methods. The marp package provides a reproducible framework for inference that accounts for model uncertainty in parametric renewal processes.

title: Transparency in Team Contracts
abstract: In contract design, the principal is often better informed about the project's chances of succeeding than the agents. To incentivize effort, the principal has two main tools: first, to design a contract, sharing part of the project's success among the agents; second, to design a (Bayesian) persuasion scheme, selectively sharing information with the agents. In this work we are interested in the optimal combination of both these tools. We tackle the joint problem through the prism of simplicity vs. optimality, and establish a stark dichotomy: The simple disclosure scheme of full transparency achieves a tight $4/3$-approximation to the optimal combination of information disclosure and team contract, when the team's production function is submodular. In contrast, full transparency can be arbitrarily far from optimal when production is supermodular. The techniques that we develop to bound the gap for submodular functions, also yield a new deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm for pure multi-agent contract design, with a significantly improved approximation ratio of $2.311$, and thus a $3.081$-approximation algorithm for the joint information and contracting problem.

title: Statistical and Privacy Guarantees for Deep M-Regression via Stochastic Gradient Langevin Dynamics
abstract: In this article, we study deep nonparametric regression trained via stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD), a variant of stochastic gradient descent that injects carefully calibrated Gaussian noise during optimization. Using a PAC-Bayesian analysis tailored to deep ReLU networks, we establish an excess-risk bound that simultaneously accounts for network approximation error, statistical complexity, and the algorithmic cost accumulated along the SGLD trajectory. Under a Bernstein condition and within a stable SGLD regime, the excess-risk bound contains a stochastic term whose coefficient is inversely proportional to the variance of injected noise, while the estimator retains the optimal rate for nonparametric regression under the H\"older smoothness condition up to logarithmic factors. This result provides an approximation-error-aware, rate-optimal statistical perspective on the widely observed generalization benefits of moderate SGLD noise. For per-sample clipped SGLD, we further establish an exact f-DP guarantee and the corresponding asymptotic $\mu$-GDP guarantee for the proposed estimator. We establish statistical convergence rates and differential privacy guarantees for DNN estimators trained using SGLD, while explicitly accounting for both network approximation error and the effect of injected noise in the excess-risk bound. Extensive simulation studies and analyses of two real datasets examine the finite-sample predictive performance and privacy-utility behavior of the proposed procedure.

title: Polynomial-Time Approximate EFX for Chores via Flow and Matching
abstract: We study approximate EFX allocations of indivisible chores under nonnegative additive costs. Exact EFX allocations need not exist in general. We develop a polynomial-time algorithm that computes a complete $(3+\varepsilon)$-EFX allocation for any rational $0<\varepsilon\leq1$, improving the previous approximation guarantee from a factor depending on the number of agents to a constant. The algorithm extends to EF$k$X, achieving a $(2+1/k+\varepsilon)$-approximation for every integer $k\geq1$. For instances with relatively few chores, the polynomial-time BRBI algorithm gives stronger guarantees. It finds exact EF$k$X allocations when $m\leq2kn$ and achieves a factor of at most $2-1/k$ when $m\le(3k-1)n$. In particular, $k=1$ and $m\leq2n$ give exact EFX. We further show that the approximation factor \(2+1/k\) is asymptotically tight for our main algorithm. We also construct a four-agent, ten-chore instance in which every complete allocation has EFX approximation factor at least $11/10$, improving upon the $20/19$ lower bound for submodular costs even under additive costs.

title: Inference after selection on randomized p-values
abstract: We consider inference on parameters and hypotheses selected using p-values. We provide a simple procedure to decompose a p-value into two components, one for inference and one for selection, that are independent under the null hypothesis. To control the Type 1 error rate conditional on selection of the null hypothesis from randomized p-values, we develop tests motivated by the selective inference approaches of data thinning, fission, and carving. Unlike the typical application of these approaches, however, our tests only make use of the p-values rather than the full data. Furthermore, we construct confidence intervals that attain the nominal conditional coverage and corresponding estimators. In the context of the file drawer problem, the winner's curse, and sequential testing, we show that our proposals offer both theoretical and empirical advantages over existing randomized and non-randomized approaches. Lastly, we apply our methods for selective inference on genetic associations using publicly-available p-values from the UK Biobank.

title: Robust prizes in all-pay contests with loss aversion
abstract: We study robust prize design in all-pay contests with loss-averse agents when the principal does not know the agents' convex cost of effort, subject to an aggregate productivity constraint. The robustly optimal prize structure awards equal prizes to all contestants except the one ranked last. The optimal bottom prize is zero under moderate loss aversion, but becomes positive and increases with loss aversion when loss aversion is sufficiently strong. Under strong loss aversion, the robust solution involves partial participation in the contest.

title: Changepoint localization via nested exchangeability tests: from point estimates to confidence intervals
abstract: We study distribution-free uncertainty quantification for a changepoint estimate in an offline setting. We observe a sequence with a single changepoint and are given an estimate of its location. The pre- and post-change segments are independent and each consists of i.i.d. (or, more generally, exchangeable) observations from arbitrary and unknown distributions. We introduce Changepoint LOcalization via Nested Exchangeability testing (CLONE), a novel method for constructing distribution-free confidence intervals around that estimate by testing exchangeability in nested windows centered at the reference estimate. Under these assumptions, CLONE provides finite-sample coverage for any black-box reference estimator. Using a geometrically shrinking radius grid, CLONE requires only $O(log n)$ permutation tests. We characterize optimal scores for the framework and provide practical recommendations that result in sharp confidence intervals. Under mild assumptions, CLONE confidence intervals have asymptotically vanishing normalized length. Simulations and experiments on image and text data support our theoretical findings.

title: A Unified Coordinate Descent Framework for Penalized Longitudinal Log-Contrast Quantile Regression
abstract: Quantile regression characterizes heterogeneous covariate effects across the response distribution, but its extension to high-dimensional longitudinal compositional data poses substantial challenges, such as the nonsmooth check loss, the unit-sum structure of compositional covariates. Existing work is confined to Lasso penalization, and does not readily extend to nonconvex penalties. We propose CDaLCqr, a unified coordinate descent algorithm for penalized longitudinal log-contrast quantile regression accommodating popular penalties, such as adaptive Lasso, smoothly clipped absolute deviation (SCAD), and minimax concave penalty (MCP) within a single framework. The proposed method uses a Huber-type smooth approximation of the check loss and enforces the zero-sum constraint through an augmented Lagrangian formulation. CDaLCqr combines coordinate descent with majorization-minimization, yielding explicit updates through coordinate-wise quadratic surrogates. We show that the stopping tolerance controls errors in the zero-sum constraint and stationarity conditions. Under suitable conditions and sufficiently close initialization, we also prove local convergence of the coefficient and multiplier iterates, with an error bound decreasing by a fixed factor less than one each iteration. Simulations highlight the estimation advantages of SCAD and MCP variants and their sparse model identification. An application to Chinese provincial industrial data identifies interpretable, quantile-specific associations between sectoral composition and regional economic output.

title: Adversarial Multiplicity: Cherry-Picked Models and the Limits of Disclosure
abstract: Predictive multiplicity -- where similarly accurate models disagree on individual predictions -- can be leveraged to optimize secondary metrics (e.g., fairness) without loss in predictive performance. However, exploiting multiplicity opens the opportunity for motivated parties (or coding agents gaming their objectives) to steer predictions toward their own ends, such as in litigation or consumer disputes with automated decision-making tools. In these adversarial multiplicity settings, we distinguish soft manipulation, where parties optimize over innocuous model choices (e.g., hyperparameter tuning, feature engineering), from hard manipulation, where parties directly perturb model parameters. We find a sufficiently flexible model can be manipulated to reverse any individual prediction with minimal change in predictive performance while passing black-box audits, making hard manipulation viable in most regulatory settings. Soft manipulation has smaller effects but can pass white-box audits requiring full access to code and data. Even aggregate estimates can be manipulated: a model's estimated effect of climate change on wildfires can be fully reversed by hard edits and soft search. We find the Reconcile algorithm typically resolves most disagreements between models, but more often in favor of the manipulator when the opposing model is chosen adversarially compared to at random. We map which manipulations can plausibly pass existing regulations and disclosure policies, and recommend mitigations such as pre-registration, proof of model training, sensitivity analyses, multi-metric evaluations, and committing to versioned public models.

title: When Do Sports Leagues Stop Being Competitive? Bayesian Detection of Competitive-Balance Eras from Match-Level Data
abstract: Competitive balance shapes outcome uncertainty, fan interest, and league regulation, yet standard measures summarize realized standings and cannot separate structural ability differences from match-level randomness. We develop a Bayesian framework that infers structural competitive balance from longitudinal match outcomes. Team abilities are obtained by projecting Gaussian auxiliary variables onto a graph-fused l1 polytope whose radius measures total pairwise ability variation. The projection places positive probability on exact ties, so statistically indistinguishable teams form explicit rank tiers. The radius equals realized ability variation whenever the constraint binds, linking it to parity, detectability, and structural inequality. An adaptive finite-regime model lets competitive eras recur, emerge, and disappear while team hierarchies remain season specific. Simulations show accurate recovery of regimes, radii, abilities, and tiers. Applied to 25 English Premier League seasons, the model identifies a persistent shift to a more stratified league beginning in 2005/06, with 2010/11 the only later return to the compressed regime. It also shows that a close title race can coexist with wide league-wide separation and that head-to-head results can separate clubs level on points. The framework gives leagues a model-based measure of balance to inform debates on revenue sharing and financial regulation.

title: ELPAC: Endpoint-Anchored Latent Progression with Stage-Varying Multimodal Coordination
abstract: Aging cohorts increasingly combine imaging, plasma, and cognitive measurements, but most subjects provide only a partially observed cross-sectional snapshot, leaving latent stage, progression subtype, and stage-varying multimodal coordination to be inferred jointly. Existing methods estimate the cohort-level aging process, model covariance under observed covariates, or fuse modalities for prediction. However, they rarely target the joint problem of endpoint-anchored staging and progression-resolved residual coordination across modalities, even though subject staging, subtype assignment, and multimodal interplay are mutually dependent. We introduce ELPAC, a Bayesian framework with two interlocking constructions. The first integrates subtype trajectories backward from clinically reliable endpoint groups along biologically structured velocity components encoding modality-specific monotone direction and optional sequential ordering priors. The second factorizes residual multimodal variation around the inferred stage axis into sparse coordination axes whose loadings and activations expose which multimodal patterns are operative in each subtype and when they emerge, with stage-resolved variation supplying the auxiliary structure for conditional identifiability. We use a scalable amortized variational inference scheme that enables joint posterior inference at cohort scale with single-pass deployment on new subjects. On synthetic data and a harmonized ADNI+NACC/SCAN Alzheimer's cohort, ELPAC demonstrates accurate latent-structure recovery, well-calibrated prediction intervals, and biologically interpretable multimodal coordination programs that differ by subtype.

title: Brave New Data: Pricing Expertise and Discovery
abstract: We study the procurement of verifiable evidence from an expert who privately assesses a binary state and chooses the direction and intensity of evidence acquisition. The buyer balances the ease of inducing discovery against its value for decisions beyond the expert's initial assessment. An optimal contract pays only for disclosed evidence, independently of the initial report. When acquisition is cheap, equal rewards for evidence of either state induce intensive search whose failure is informative. As costs rise, rewarding evidence of only one state becomes optimal despite the symmetry of the environment, reducing expected payments at the expense of decision accuracy.

title: Clouded Representatives and Score Matching for Distributed Quantile Regression
abstract: Quantile regression is widely used in high-stakes applications where the data are distributed across many sites and the individual records cannot be shared. The existing distributed methods for quantile regression typically require homogeneous sites, large sites, or synchronous communication, which are rarely all satisfied in practice. In this paper, we propose a new method named cloudqr. Each site summarizes its observations by a few Gaussian clouds, each given by the size, center, and covariance of a group of observations, such that the clouds match the score of the raw data exactly. A central server then fits the quantile regression on the clouds from all sites. We establish the convergence of cloudqr under mild conditions. With simulation studies and two real-world applications, we demonstrate the superior performance of cloudqr over the existing distributed methods.

title: Double Machine Learning for Panel Data: Identification, Specification, and a Bank Regulation Effect
abstract: This paper examines robustness and causal interpretation of panel estimates using double/debiased machine learning. The prototype treatment setup is the 2018 US banking regulation. Under common treatment timing, we characterize identification and nuisance restrictions and derive exact bank-level representations of specified "within" and "first-difference" scores. Simulations assess panel model transformation-induced specification bias and inference under weaker overlap. Empirically, estimates vary with asset-size classification and prior growth. Prior-growth adjustment reduces overlap-weighted estimates across four Machine Learners (ML); doubly robust estimates depend on the fitted propensity and concentrated weights. Both bank groups received relief, so we estimate differential exposure effects. The findings highlight specification issues and the relation between functional-form robustness and causal identification.

title: Nonparametric Subgraph Regression
abstract: Estimation and inference on a single large network are challenging due to dependence among observations. This paper studies nonparametric regression for outcomes defined on groups of $p$ agents, such as the indicator that three agents in a network form a triangle. Outcomes on groups that share an agent may be dependent, while outcomes on disjoint groups are independent. I call this problem subgraph regression; it nests dyadic regression as the special case $p=2$. Its leading application concerns subgraphs of a network, but the methods apply to any outcome defined on groups of agents. I establish a variance bound, uniform convergence rates in probability, and pointwise asymptotic normality for the subgraph analogue of the Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression estimator. The setting differs from regression with i.i.d. data in two ways: (i) the number of observations, of order $N^p$, overstates the effective sample size, which is $N$, and (ii) the rate of convergence depends on the dimension of the covariates of a single agent rather than of all $p$ agents, which mitigates the curse of dimensionality.

title: Neyman Orthogonalized Specification Tests for Conditional Tail Index Models
abstract: We develop specification tests for parametric conditional tail index models of heavy-tailed distributions. The tests are based on a projected empirical process that removes the first-order effect of estimating the null parameter. Within the conditional Hall class, we identify conditions under which projection also eliminates the leading Pareto approximation bias in the test process, permitting lower thresholds while preserving asymptotically correct size. We establish the validity of the tests via multiplier bootstrap. For log-linear models, bootstrap validity extends to settings in which covariates among observations above a common threshold concentrate and the smallest eigenvalue of the information matrix tends to zero. We further propose a data-driven threshold selection rule based on an estimate of the Pareto approximation bias after projection. The rule allows lower thresholds to retain more observations for testing while limiting size distortions, with potential gains in power. The finite sample performance of the tests is examined through simulations and a real data application.

title: Sample size calculation comparing two survival curves in the presence of nonproportional hazards utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time using two different Weibull distributions
abstract: Sample size calculations in two-arm clinical trials with survival endpoint often utilize the proportional hazards (PH) assumption. In case of nonproportional hazards (NPH), much research is ongoing with some newer methods developed that work well in specific scenarios. Recent developments have considered the nonparametric Max-Combo logrank test for both design and analysis of survival data with NPH. Although many approaches have been proposed for analyzing time-to-event data with NPH such as Restricted Mean Survival Time, Average Hazard Ratios, and piecewise exponential model with hazard ratios changing over time, translation into sample size calculation is not obvious and relies on simulations for very specific scenarios of NPH. In the parametric setting, accelerated failure time models that allow NPH but require a constant time ratio assumption (PT assumption) have been proposed. Recently, a parametric approach that simultaneously allows both nonproportional hazards (NPH) and nonproportional time (NPT) has been proposed. It utilizes the concept of Relative Time (RT) with two different Weibull distributions for the two trial arms in the case of monotonically increasing/decreasing time ratios. A key limitation is that the hypotheses leading to the sample size calculation rely on a single effect size defined at a specific survival percentile. In our current work, we extend the parent RT method by utilizing the concept of Weighted Relative Time (WRT) that allows us comparison of the full survival curves. Performance of the proposed method is compared to the Max-Combo method under different weighting schemes, and its operation characteristics are studied via simulations.

title: Complex Menus in Discriminatory Pricing
abstract: Advances in technology decrease the costs of offering and choosing from large menus of varieties. As these complexity costs fall, how large are the menus offered by monopolists likely to become? For the multi-product or multi-attribute case, ubiquitous in practice, we show that optimal menus are generically infinite in the absence of complexity costs. Complexity costs can decrease the menu size, but it grows without bound as these costs decrease. These results have no analogue in the single-dimensional model and do not rely on non-linearities in production costs or preferences; the extensive product differentiation is caused by screening considerations alone.

title: dsp: An R Package for Bayesian Time Series Modeling with the Dynamic Shrinkage Process
abstract: dsp provides a unified state-space framework for modeling nonstationary time series using the Dynamic Shrinkage Process (DSP), a class of global-local shrinkage priors. DSP adaptively regularizes time-varying parameters to shrink noise while preserving abrupt changes and other local structure. The package supports Gaussian and count-data smoothing, changepoint detection, time-varying parameter regression, and volatility estimation, with posterior predictive draws available for missing-value imputation and forecasting. Nonstationary time series often contain periods of relative stability punctuated by abrupt changes in mean or variance. dsp offers a common interface for model specification, posterior computation, summarization, and visualization across models that were previously developed separately in the literature. Core functionality is implemented in C++ via Rcpp for computational efficiency. We describe the underlying models, package design, and the main functions for fitting, summarizing, and plotting posterior results.

title: Polynomial-Time Computation of Extensive-Form Proper Equilibria in Two-Player Zero-Sum Games
abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for computing an exact extensive-form proper equilibrium in a finite two-player zero-sum extensive-form game with perfect recall and rational data. Properness is understood in the agent normal form: an action at an information set is penalized relative to a better action while all other local behavioral choices, including the player's own future actions, remain fixed. Our algorithm assigns each information set a geometric permutahedron of allowable action probabilities. A scaled doubly stochastic representation embeds these restrictions in a polynomial-size sequence-form polytope; a saddle point then satisfies the local $\varepsilon$-properness inequalities. To obtain an exact equilibrium rather than a solution at an arbitrarily small numerical perturbation, we establish sign stability of a parametric linear system, construct a persistent feasible basis, and extract the limits of behavioral ratios. The resulting probabilities are rational and have polynomial encoding length, including at information sets whose realization probabilities vanish.

title: Optimistic Hedge in General-Sum Games: Fundamental Limits and Regret Bounds via Temporal Approximation
abstract: Optimistic Hedge, a multiplicative weight update with one step of extrapolation, is one of the most natural regret-minimizing dynamics for games, and characterizing its regret has been a longstanding open question. Daskalakis, Fishelson and Golowich proved that if all $m$ players in a finite general-sum game follow Optimistic Hedge with a fixed learning rate, each player's regret is polylogarithmic in the horizon $T$. Subsequently, Ha showed that an appropriate choice of learning rate makes each player's regret bounded independently of $T$. This bound, however, is non-constructive and its dependence on the number of actions $n$ is not explicit, leaving open whether Optimistic Hedge can achieve a constant regret bound which is polynomial in the size of the game. We show that the answer hinges on the number of players. In two-player games, there is a learning rate for which Optimistic Hedge guarantees $O(n\log n)$ regret independent of the horizon. In three-player games, however, no such bound is possible: for any learning rate up to an absolute constant and for sufficiently large horizon $T$, there is a game with $n$ actions per player in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(n)}$, and more generally, for every $m\ge3$ we construct $m$-player games in which some player's regret is $2^{\Omega(mn)}$; for learning rates above $2^{-\Omega(mn)}$, that player's regret even grows linearly in $T$. Our upper bound is based on a temporal approximation framework for the analysis of Optimistic Hedge. Starting from the variance-based RVU bound of Daskalakis et al., we approximate the losses over time-localized windows by well-behaved functions, whose total variation is a small fraction of their cumulative variance. In $m$-player games, the same framework gives a significantly simplified proof of the recent $O(\sqrt{m}\log n\log T)$ regret bound due to Ha.

title: Online Edge-Weighted Matching Beyond 0.55
abstract: We give a $0.556195$-competitive randomized algorithm for edge-weighted online bipartite matching with free disposal, improving the $0.5368$ guarantee of Blanc and Charikar. The result holds for arbitrary nonnegative edge weights and any input sequence fixed independently of the algorithm's randomness. Our algorithm builds on online correlated selection, introduced by Fahrbach, Huang, Tao, and Zadimoghaddam, and its multiway extension due to Blanc and Charikar. Our main contribution is a state-dependent primal--dual analysis of correlated selection. At each weight threshold, we track the state of the selection process jointly with an auxiliary failure event. The analysis accounts for arrivals below the threshold, which change the state without improving the matching value at that threshold. A potential function bounds the dual increase in both cases. We instantiate the analysis with an explicit win map that assigns a common score to an initial range of states. Its selection inequalities are verified by a finite computer-assisted proof covering every required candidate multiplicity and every real threshold; the verifiers are available in an accompanying repository. Triangular unit-weight inputs asymptotically attain the guarantee of the underlying ideal algorithm, proving that its analysis is tight.

title: Prophet Secretary for Matroids and XOS Valuations: A Separation at 1-1/e and a 0.6767 Guarantee for I.I.D. Weights
abstract: Ehsani, Hajiaghayi, Kesselheim, and Singla (SODA 2018) give $(1-1/e)$-competitive algorithms for matroid prophet-secretary and prophet-secretary with XOS valuation functions. In this work we show that these two guarantees have different limits. For every matroid, we give a randomized $(1-1/e+\varepsilon_0)$-competitive algorithm, where $\varepsilon_0=10^{-6}$. The guarantee holds for independent nonnegative values with finite expected optimum. For explicitly given finite distributions with rational values and probabilities, the algorithm has polynomial worst-case running time in the matroid independence-oracle model. The oracle tests whether a queried set is independent. The algorithm makes $O(N^4)$ such queries in expectation and $O(N^4\log(N+2))$ in the worst case, where $N$ is the number of elements. We further consider the i.i.d. version of this problem and provide a $0.6767$ competitive ratio for every matroid with i.i.d.\ nonnegative weights from a known distribution. This guarantee even holds in fixed arrival order (a.k.a. i.i.d. matriod prophet inequalities), even when the algorithm learns the order only as the elements arrive. For combinatorial auctions with XOS valuations, however, we show that $1-1/e$ is the optimal competitive ratio. We give an explicit family of finite instances showing that no online algorithm can guarantee a larger competitive ratio than $1-1/e$, even when the buyers' valuations are i.i.d., every additive clause has coefficients in $\{0,1\}$, and computation is unrestricted. Thus the matroid improvement exploits structure absent from general allocation with XOS valuations.

title: Dull, Dirty, Dangerous? Working Conditions and the Limits of Occupational AI Exposure
abstract: Automation is often justified as relief from dull, dirty, and dangerous work. I examine how these conditions relate to occupational AI exposure using 21 O*NET items across 754 US occupations. Higher exposure is associated with lower condition scores under a large language model (LLM) measure and AI Occupational Exposure (AIOE), with equal occupation weights and employment weights. Adjustment for physical demands, required education, training and experience, and wages reduces the composite association. The adjusted confidence intervals include zero for LLM exposure and remain below zero for AIOE. Separating repetition from restricted discretion also changes what the combined Dull score conveys. These comparisons show how item groupings and occupational characteristics shape the interpretation of exposure estimates. Occupational profiles offer a starting point for selecting contrasting research settings. Establishing desired automation or realized relief requires evidence about workers' preferences and specific interventions.

title: Regression with Many Generated Controls
abstract: We consider linear regression when some covariates are endogenous, a variable sufficient to control for endogeneity exists but is latent, and the practitioner can generate many proxies for the latent control. For instance, one could cheaply but imperfectly impute the latent control using different AI/ML methods, each generating a different proxy. There are several options the practitioner might consider in this scenario: including all proxies or factors computed from the proxies as controls, instrumental variables estimation, and some nonlinear variants thereof. We use a transparent model to derive the implicit estimand each approach targets, determine when these estimands recover the parameter of interest, and provide some practical recommendations. We show that with a sufficiently rich set of generated controls, practitioners can consistently estimate the parameter of interest without relying on validation data.

title: Inherited Local Shrinkage for Adaptive Functional Form Discovery
authors: Jacob C. Schultz and Daniel Taylor-Rodriguez
abstract: Statistical models frequently employ nonlinear effects, interactions, and multiresolution basis expansions to represent complex relationships between predictors and responses. Determining the appropriate level of model complexity, however, remains a fundamental challenge. This paper introduces \textit{Inherited Local Shrinkage} (ILS), a Bayesian global-local shrinkage framework for adaptive functional form discovery that incorporates strong heredity among hierarchically related predictors. ILS propagates shrinkage through directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) encoding relationships among predictors, allowing increasingly complex terms to contribute only when supported by their simpler ancestors. This construction provides a common prior framework for a broad class of hierarchical regression models. We demonstrate its application to polynomial regression, as well as multiresolution modeling with two-dimensional Haar wavelet and eigenvalue-ordered spline (EVOS) bases. Although these examples illustrate specific basis systems, ILS is not tied to any particular basis construction and can be applied to any regression model in which relationships among predictors can be represented by a DAG, regardless of the graph's size or topology. Simulation studies demonstrate that ILS achieves competitive predictive performance relative to existing heredity-constrained methods while recovering underlying functional structure. Spatial applications further illustrate its ability to adaptively regulate model complexity across multiple resolutions, identifying where finer-scale detail is supported by the data. Together, these results establish ILS as a flexible framework for hierarchical complexity control and adaptive functional form discovery in Bayesian regression.

title: Stability and Perfection in Constrained Weighted Network Games
abstract: We introduce a general framework of constrained weighted network formation in which agents allocate resources across coalitional interactions while facing feasibility constraints. More precisely, we allow arbitrary coalitions of agents to be assigned a continuous weight, and we incorporate both coalitional capacity constraints and individual budget constraints into the model. This framework extends the weighted network formation model of Bich and Morhaim by combining continuous interaction intensities with endogenous feasibility restrictions. Within this setting, we introduce a new notion of stability -- called coalitionwise stability -- extending pairwise stability to constrained network games. Under standard continuity and componentwise quasiconcavity assumptions on payoff functions, we establish the existence of coalitionwise stable networks. We then investigate refinements of stability inspired by the notion of perfect equilibrium introduced by Selten, and by the notion of perfect pairwise stability developed by Bich and Teteryatnikova for network games. The presence of feasibility constraints fundamentally alters the geometry of the feasible set, which no longer possesses a product structure. As a consequence, trembling-hand type refinements become substantially more delicate, since perturbations of some interactions may render other interactions infeasible. Nevertheless, we introduce constrained analogues of both the trembling-hand and perturbative notions of perfect stability considered by Bich and Teteryatnikova, and study their existence and their relationship. In particular, we show the equivalence between these trembling-hand and perturbative formulations under some componentwise monotonicity assumption.

title: You Know What You Will Like: People Predict Their Own Ratings Better Than Recommender Systems
abstract: Recommender systems usually learn what people want from what they have done. Platforms could also ask people directly, but asking is costly: 98.8% of the prompts in our data went unanswered. Theories of statistical prediction imply that a person's own forecast adds little to a recommender algorithm built from many people's behavior. Theories of dispersed knowledge imply that people hold information about their own taste that the data lack. We test the two with the MovieLens Beliefs dataset. In 2023-2024, a homepage prompt asked members how they expected to rate movies they said they had not seen. Of 26,020 such expectations, 551 from 277 members were followed by a rating at least a day later. We compare each expectation with four benchmarks: the platform's own predicted rating, two collaborative-filtering models (matrix factorization and an item neighborhood), and a stack trained on other members' outcomes. The trained models use each member's latest ratings. People predict their own ratings more accurately than all four benchmarks (correlation 0.69, against 0.34 for MovieLens and 0.54 to 0.59 for the trained recommenders). Added to all the machine forecasts and features, the expectation lowers out-of-sample mean squared error by 26%. The gain holds when models are trained on earlier expectations and tested on later ones. A member's earlier expectations about other movies do not replace the current one. In ordering a member's own movies, the trained recommenders are statistically indistinguishable from the person. On old, heavily rated movies, the machines do as well or better. The results reconcile the two theories: the crowd's data suffice where they are rich, and the person adds information about the specific item. We derive four design principles for preference elicitation and recommender evaluation.

title: Universal Nonexistence of Monotone Equilibrium in Multiunit Auctions with Risk Aversion
abstract: We establish universal nonexistence results for monotone pure-strategy equilibrium in multiunit auctions with risk-averse bidders. Fix any number of bidders greater than one and any profile of strictly increasing concave utilities, with at least one strictly risk-averse bidder. Under uniform pricing, for every supply of at least three units, we construct independent, full-support type distributions under which neither lowest-winning-bid nor highest-losing-bid pricing admits an admissible monotone equilibrium. Under discriminatory pricing, we construct a finite supply and independent, full-support type distributions that preclude monotone pure-strategy equilibrium. We extend these results to all-pay auctions and finite bid grids.

title: Tight bounds for fractional and randomized truthful scheduling
abstract: We resolve one of the longest-standing open problems in algorithmic mechanism design by showing that randomization cannot yield a sublinear approximation for truthful scheduling on unrelated machines, even when truthfulness is required only in expectation. Our main technical result concerns fractional scheduling, where tasks may be split among machines. We prove that every deterministic truthful fractional mechanism on $n$ unrelated machines has worst-case approximation ratio at least $(n+1)/2$, even against the optimal integral makespan. This matches the known upper bound exactly and settles the optimal approximation ratio of truthful fractional scheduling. Since the expected allocations and payments of a truthful-in-expectation mechanism define a truthful fractional mechanism, the same lower bound applies to all truthful-in-expectation mechanisms and, in particular, to all universally truthful mechanisms. On the positive side, we give a universally truthful mechanism with approximation ratio $n/2+o(n)$. Together, these results establish the optimal leading constant $1/2$ for randomized truthful scheduling. Thus, randomization improves on the optimal deterministic approximation ratio by an asymptotic factor of two, and no more.

title: Does Frontier AI Strengthen Cyber Defense? Evidence from Project Glasswing
abstract: Defenders and attackers race to find the same software flaws. I use the launch of Project Glasswing, which gave a small group of large US tech firms early access to Claude Mythos Preview, a model for finding software vulnerabilities, to study how access to frontier AI affects defenders, external researchers, and attackers. Using the universe of publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, I find that firms with access more than doubled their disclosures relative to Chinese and Russian tech firms without access, disclosed about 150 percent more high-impact vulnerabilities, and fixed reported flaws as quickly as before. As treated firms found more flaws themselves, external researchers, who sell their findings through bug bounties, reported about half as many vulnerabilities in treated firms' code and more in other firms' code, without leaving the market. There is no evidence that attackers exploited the additional vulnerabilities: the share exploited within a month of disclosure fell by about two thirds, mainly because a smaller share was already exploited when disclosed, while the number exploited did not change. Frontier AI helped defenders find and fix more flaws before attackers exploited them, but its restricted release creates an asymmetry in software security between firms in different countries.

title: Weak Atomic Continuity and Subgame Perfection
abstract: Subgame-perfect equilibrium need not exist in continuous games with perfect information when Nature moves. Under standard regularity assumptions, we prove that weak atomic continuity of Nature's transition probabilities yields a measurable pure-strategy subgame-perfect equilibrium for finite and infinite horizons. The condition, originating in the population genetics literature, is necessary for the existence of subgame-perfect equilibrium uniformly over the remaining primitives: whenever this condition is violated, one can construct a dynamic game with no subgame-perfect equilibrium, even in behavioral strategies. The proof preserves compactness and upper hemicontinuity of continuation payoff correspondences under integration without requiring convexity.

title: On Competing Sellers with Substitutable Goods
abstract: We study mechanism design by an incumbent seller facing competition from an entrant seller of a substitute good. The incumbent commits to a potentially randomized mechanism before her competitor responds. A unit-demand buyer with fixed, publicly known values for the two goods observes both mechanisms and may interact with them in either order. How should a revenue-maximizing incumbent design her mechanism when her product is superior or inferior to her competitor's? We determine the incumbent's exact optimal revenue and characterize all mechanisms that obtain it. Commitment and randomization allow her to earn strictly positive revenue even against an arbitrarily superior product, despite earning nothing under posted-price (i.e., Bertrand) competition. Optimal mechanisms can require a continuum of lottery options, even though the buyer selects only one in equilibrium: unselected options shape the competitor's incentives rather than screen private buyer information. We also show that the buyer's ability to choose the interaction order can be strictly beneficial to the incumbent, even though the incumbent is always visited first at equilibrium. Finally, we show that without commitment, every pure Nash equilibrium yields Bertrand revenues even with randomized mechanisms.

title: Competitive Equilibrium for Linear Chores is CLS-complete
abstract: The competitive equilibrium (CE) is a fundamental concept for markets, with applications to efficient and fair allocation of resources. We consider the fundamental question of computing a CE in the most basic Fisher market model where agents have linear preferences. While it is known that we can compute a CE in strongly polynomial time with linear goods, there is no known polynomial-time algorithm for CE with linear chores. Computing a CE for linear chores is known to be in CLS with no hardness results. In this paper, we prove that computing an exact CE in Fisher markets with divisible chores and linear disutilities is CLS-hard and thus CLS-complete. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first CLS-completeness result for a market equilibrium problem. On the technical side, we use the nonconvex dual Eisenberg-Gale (EG) program whose Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) points are CE [Chaudhury, Kroer, Mehta, and Nan, 2024], and the CLS-complete problem of computing a KKT point of a quadratic program [Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender, and Savani, 2024]. We show that from any exact equilibrium of the constructed market, we can recover in polynomial time an $\varepsilon$-KKT point of the input quadratic program over the unit box.

title: Approximate minimax regret for conditionally similar tests
abstract: We construct approximately minimax regret optimal tests in a scalar Gaussian instrumental variables experiment. This example shows how conditionally similar tests allow a novel approximation approach, allowing us to optimize weights over alternatives to minimize worst-case power regret. Stochastic mirror descent and averaging yield finite-iteration guarantees with exact conditional similarity. We establish bounds for exact and simulated powers and illustrate the procedure numerically. This initial algorithm shows how existing nearly-optimal test computation methods can be extended to include composite alternative hypothesis sets without the computational cost associated with maintaining size control.

title: Online Control of the Family-wise Error Rate (FWER) for Multi-stage Platform Trials
abstract: In platform trials, multiple intervention arms can enter or leave the study at any time, which brings the challenge of how to control the type I error rate. Online testing procedures, where a stream of hypotheses are tested over time and the total number of hypotheses is unknown, might be a viable choice for error rate control in platform trials. Interim analyses in a multi-stage design offer the opportunity of early stopping for success or futility in clinical trials by testing the same hypothesis at different time points. Some methods targeting false-discovery rate (FDR) or family-wise error rate (FWER) control for multi-stage platform trials have been proposed. However, a method which controls the FWER and allows new arms to be added at any time without prior information is yet to be established. The ADDIS-Spending (ADaptive DIScarding Alpha-spending) procedure controls the FWER in an online setting. We propose the group sequential ADDIS-Spending algorithm to enable interim analyses for each hypothesis in platform trials. The developed method can update the error level of an individual hypothesis at all (interim) analyses whenever new decisions on other hypotheses are made. We compare alternative approaches with our method in a simulation study. The proposed method yields competitive results in the conducted simulations.

title: An Interaction-Aware Decision Framework for FDIC-Assisted Distressed Bank Acquisitions: Empirical Evidence from the FDIC Failed-Bank Panel and the SVB-First Citizens Case
abstract: Acquirers of failed banks weigh acquisition value, regulatory protection, risk, buyer strength, and execution difficulty jointly, because each signal's meaning depends on the others: high non-performing loans matter less when government loss sharing absorbs the losses. The proposed Spider Network Filtering Framework encodes such dependencies as four interpretable interaction rules among five dimensions, yielding graph-inspired features for a logistic model and a Pursue/Caution/Avoid decision rule. We evaluate it on 55 acquisitions assisted by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation in 2008-2024 by acquirers with a parent listed in the United States. Six financial inputs come from regulatory reports published before each failure; two deal terms, which the winning bidder knows when it bids but investors learn at the announcement, come from the regulator's press releases. The outcome, a positive three-day abnormal return around the announcement, records the market's initial reception, not realized success. Under grouped, nested cross-validation, the Spider-enhanced model reaches a mean area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.594, against 0.615 for logistic regression on the same inputs and 0.632 for ridge regression; permutation tests that repeat the full model selection give at most weak evidence that any of them ranks better than chance. The Spider score used directly does not rank better than chance, and an apparent link between target distress and higher returns disappears against a bank-sector benchmark.
