Towards the goal of better understanding these systems from a social choice perspective, we introduce two frameworks that encompass existing desiderata for majoritarian and proportional settings: coalitions, which encompasses properties such as fixed majority and solid coalitions; and stability, which encompasses various generalizations of Condorcet's criterion for single-winner elections, such as Gehrlein stability and local stability, among others. We develop theory and tools that characterize the mathematical and computational aspects of both frameworks across a wide array of preference structures (such as the unrestricted domain over candidates and the restricted domain of party lists). Building on this foundation, we shed new light on majority jackpot electoral systems, which to date have received limited mathematical analysis in the social choice literature.

title: Metric Subtraction for Non-Euclidean Random Objects with Applications to Residual Analysis
abstract: Residual analysis for non-Euclidean regression models is challenging due to the lack of a natural subtraction operation and a corresponding notion of conditionally centered residuals. We introduce a metric subtraction framework that yields residuals in the original response space, with their conditional Fr\'echet mean equal to a fixed reference object when the model is correctly specified. We establish sufficient conditions for this conditional centering property, together with a separate condition ensuring distance preservation, providing a construction principle for suitable metric subtraction operators. The proposed metric subtraction framework accommodates several important classes of metric spaces, including spheres, symmetric positive definite matrices, simplices, and Wasserstein spaces. Building on this framework, we develop a randomized test for detecting remaining conditional location effects and establish its asymptotic size and power against fixed alternatives. We further introduce two complementary diagnostic tools, signed distance plots and distance-profile-based boxplots, to visualize systematic residual patterns and identify atypical observations. For uncertainty quantification, we construct residual-based prediction sets and establish their asymptotic validity. Simulation studies and applications to New York City bicycle usage distributions and U.S. electricity generation compositions demonstrate the practical utility of the proposed framework for model assessment, residual diagnostics, and prediction in non-Euclidean regression.

title: Owning What Can Quit
abstract: Academic journals are part of the infrastructure of science, yet most journal titles are owned by commercial publishers while their standing rests on editors and boards who can leave. This paper asks what that separation means for the governance of science. Using a coded dataset of all 57 editorial mass resignations recorded by Retraction Watch from 2015 to 2026, data on editor tenure at 110 economics, finance and accounting journals, and journal-level publication and revenue data, I document three patterns. First, resignation does not reverse an owner's decision: in none of the 19 episodes involving an editor's replacement did the owner back down after the board resigned, so editorial communities have influence only before they leave. Second, whether a departing board can take a journal's standing with it depends on institutions outside the board: successor journals follow most often where a scholarly society backs the board and rarely in medicine, where non-profit hosts are scarce, while journal ranking lists, which rate titles rather than the people who edit them, keep reputation with the owner. Third, a stated limit on editor tenure was applied at the publisher's discretion; where it was applied, output grew almost fourfold, a short-run gain whose long-run effect on the journal's standing is not yet known. I draw implications for scholarly societies, funders, publishers, and the bodies that compile journal rankings.

title: RATSIFT: Resolution-Adaptive Transformer for Solar Irradiance Forecasting and Temporal Downscaling
abstract: Accurate forecasting and temporal downscaling of solar irradiance is critical for reliable renewable energy integration and grid management. Traditional methods often struggle to capture rapid irradiance variability. In this work, we develop a Transformer-based architecture for simultaneous forecasting and temporal downscaling. The model takes input data at arbitrary resolutions and generates outputs at any resolutions represented within the training data, leveraging both global and local contextual information. To improve training efficiency, a genetic algorithm-based optimization framework is implemented to identify suitable model hyperparameters, while reducing the computational cost of exhaustive grid search. The effectiveness of the proposed model is shown by analyzing real data in Dallas, Texas. The proposed model achieved root mean square error (RMSE) values of 28.785, 29.544, 30.157, 32.132~W/m\(^2\) for 15-, 30-, 60-minute, and irregularly spaced global input and producing forecast at 5-minutes resolution, respectively. Furthermore, this model produced reliable uncertainty estimates, exhibiting wider prediction intervals for high-resolution inputs during volatile solar conditions, whereas coarser-resolution inputs result in narrower intervals and significantly lower training time and computational cost. Our approach provides a scalable and efficient framework for multi-resolution solar irradiance forecasting and temporal downscaling, suitable for practical energy forecasting and grid management applications.

title: Why Good Experience Can End Joint Activity
abstract: Learning a partner's preferences through joint activity can make both partners worse off than receiving no feedback from the activity. We study a responder who values the partner's payoff but bears a cost when joining is attributed to personal interest. Both partners observe noisy evidence of whether the responder wanted the activity, available only after participation. Evidence of interest raises this cost, discouraging joining on unwanted days; joining only on wanted days would then be too revealing to sustain. With choices based on current payoffs, we derive a condition under which learning can end participation without ever making stopping beneficial to either partner. Feedback accuracy and preference persistence described by couples' diaries satisfy this condition at baseline payoffs. Once activity stops, no further evidence arrives and the belief that the responder generally wants the activity stays fixed, so waiting may never restore it; preference information available without participating can. A separate forward-looking model with highly persistent preferences shows why this remedy can also reduce joint welfare. When participation reveals preferences exactly, a responder may accept at a current loss to establish a lack of interest, making acceptance less revealing and so sustaining participation on wanted days. Free daily revelation outside the activity removes this incentive. At the model's baseline, it lowers the best joint value in monotone Markov equilibria with exact participation feedback, but raises it with feedback as weak as the diary's.

title: The Verification Bottleneck
abstract: This paper studies how generative AI, by lowering the cost of research production, affects scientific verification in a general-equilibrium model of peer review. Privately informed researchers choose observable output, an editor optimally assigns review depth, and reviewers supply time according to its expected scientific contribution. Costly output helps screen research quality, and cheaper production lets weaker researchers imitate stronger ones more readily. Beyond a technological threshold, reviewer capacity and verified knowledge weakly decline even under optimal editorial decisions, and strictly when a screening constraint has positive shadow value. Reviewer withdrawal can amplify the loss. With observable quality, the same progress weakly increases both.

title: Partial Invariance for Classification under Structural Causal Models
abstract: Making predictions in an unseen environment from data collected across multiple training environments is challenging. This challenge is particularly pronounced when the target-generating mechanism varies across environments. In this work, we introduce environment-label separation, a form of partial environmental invariance that decomposes the target conditional distribution into an environment-invariant component and a label-invariant component. We show that this partial invariance enables estimation of the target conditional distribution in an unseen environment when using labeled training data together with unlabeled test features. Within the structural causal model framework, we provide sufficient conditions for environment-label separation. Building on these conditions, we develop an algorithm, dIMP-Classifier, which jointly minimizes an estimate of the test risk and encourages invariance across environments. We further provide finite-sample guarantees that characterize the test risk in terms of deviations from invariance, estimation error, and sample complexity. Experiments on simulated data and the real-world light tunnel Causal Chamber data demonstrate that the proposed approach can perform under interventions on the target mechanism and consistently outperforms the considered standard and invariance-based baselines.

title: A General Approach for Assessing Sensitivity to Violations of Causal Assumptions
abstract: Although causal sensitivity analyses are widely used to assess the robustness of conclusions, a key limitation is that existing methods are typically developed for specific designs. This paper develops a general sensitivity analysis framework that applies to a wide range of discrete causal models and estimands by deriving sharp bounds on causal estimands as a function of the maximum proportion of the population for which the assumption is relaxed. The framework is built on the generalized principal strata approach, which allows the translation of assumptions, estimands, and data into polynomial programs. In this approach, three classes of assumptions can be relaxed: a) functional restrictions, which limit the ways that one variable can respond to another, e.g. strong monotonicity; b) exclusion restrictions, which rule out direct causal effects; c) unconfoundedness, which rules out unobserved common causes of variables. The approach produces both sharp sensitivity curves and robustness values, i.e., the smallest sensitivity level at which the sign of a causal effect stops being identified. The applicability of the method is demonstrated by generalizing existing proportion-of-violations approaches, deriving new sensitivity analysis methods for instrumental variable and selection-on-observables designs, and reanalyzing empirical results.

title: Empirical rather than simulated spectral band adjustment of MODIS to Sentinel-3 OLCI for European vegetation monitoring
abstract: Spectral band adjustment derived from convolved spectra describes sensor differences under controlled conditions, but its applicability to operational products requires assessment. We compare this approach with adjustment estimated directly from MODIS and Sentinel-3 OLCI observations for European vegetation monitoring. Both streams undergo atmospheric correction and Ross-Thick/Li-Sparse Reciprocal BRDF normalization to nadir viewing and local solar noon. Using observations from 2019-2024, we derive annual OLCI/MODIS reflectance-ratio relationships with unadjusted MODIS NDVI. The operational correction uses quadratic red and linear near-infrared (NIR) functions. We compare these relationships with irradiance-weighted canopy simulations and assess the empirical correction at 460 locations. Simulated and empirical relationships differ, particularly for red reflectance at high NDVI. Background-dependent simulated ratios also demonstrate the limitations of a single NDVI-based function. The empirical correction reduces red and NIR root-mean-square error (RMSE) at 66.3% and 71.1% of locations, with median paired reductions of 5.98% and 13.67%. Median paired RMSE decreases by 0.86% for NDVI but increases by 0.95% for EVI2, 0.74% for NIRv and 7.07% for the Plant Phenology Index (PPI), calculated with stream-specific historical references. This study establishes an operational empirical adjustment and shows that the specified spectral simulation does not reproduce the relationship between the normalized products. It provides evidence for improved reflectance consistency while demonstrating that vegetation-index benefits require separate assessment.

title: Directional Nonlinear Principal Components: a measure transportation approach
abstract: One of the earliest techniques in multivariate analysis, Principal Component Analysis (PCA) remains among the most popular ones in the area. PCA, however, is a linear and bidirectional technique (principal directions $\pm\mathbf{u}$ are defined up to a sign), which is fine under Gaussian or elliptical assumptions but constitutes a major limitation outside that restrictive context. This has prompted the development of numerous nonlinear approaches. We show here how recent results in measure transportation allow for a nonlinear and strictly directional (disentangling $\mathbf{u}$ and $-\mathbf{u}$) concept preserving the intuitive interpretation of the classical linear concept by maximizing expected squared arc lengths along data-driven principal curves rather than principal directions.

title: A multivariate unsupervised lognormal-GPD mixture for dependent losses
abstract: We propose a multivariate two-population mixture distribution for heavy-tailed and positively skewed non-negative data. The first mixture population is a multivariate lognormal, while the second is a distribution obtained by joining univariate zero-mean generalized Pareto densities via a Gumbel copula. The model is unsupervised, since no threshold has to be set or estimated. We derive some properties of the distribution and develop an Expectation-Conditional Maximization algorithm for maximum likelihood estimation, which is found to perform well in multivariate contexts beyond the bivariate case. The finite-sample properties of the estimators are assessed by means of simulation experiments, and an empirical application to aggregated commercial property-casualty insurance claims illustrates the impact of dependence on risk estimation. All the methods are implemented in the R package MultLognGPD, available on Github.

title: Optimal spectral shrinkage via Krylov approximation
abstract: Spectral shrinkage encompasses a broad family of estimators for high-dimensional linear regression that regularize estimation and prediction by applying spectral filters to the sample covariance matrix. Despite its widespread use, achieving oracle-optimal prediction risk under general covariance structures remains challenging, as the oracle filter requires unknown population quantities and has a closed form only for specific covariance models such as isotropic and spiked models. We propose \textit{risk-targeted Krylov fitting} (RTK), a data-driven spectral estimator that adapts to the unknown covariance structure and attains the oracle risk asymptotically. Like partial least squares, RTK operates in an $m$-dimensional Krylov space, but it targets the oracle risk directly by minimizing the leave-one-out risk, which we compute exactly without refitting the model $n$ times. Under general distributions and covariance structures, RTK attains the optimal prediction risk in the Krylov space up to $O(1/n)$. Furthermore, its risk approaches that of the optimal analytic filter with $m$ of order $\log n$. In simulations over a wide range of covariance structures, RTK and a truncated variant were robust to the choice of $m$ and consistently among the spectral estimators closest to the oracle. In applications to single-cell sequencing data and large-scale neural recordings, the proposed methods achieved higher prediction accuracy than competing estimators on most tasks.

title: Looking Forward to Constructing Better Causal Comparisons
abstract: Constructing credible comparison groups is a central challenge in observational causal inference. Conventional approaches assess comparability through observed characteristics or pre-treatment outcome trajectories, although causal identification depends on unobserved untreated potential outcomes after treatment. We propose a forward-looking framework that selects or weights controls using prognostic scores: predictions, based on pre-treatment information, of the outcomes units would experience without treatment. These scores target either untreated outcome levels or changes, depending on the comparability condition underlying the causal design. They can be estimated using post-treatment outcomes observed for untreated units or exclusively from historical data. To construct these scores, we leverage tabular foundation models, whose extensive pretraining enables them to capture complex relationships among predictors and effectively extract their predictive information, even when application-specific samples are limited. Crucially, predictions guide comparison-group construction, whereas observed outcomes determine treatment effect estimates. We derive an exact decomposition of estimation error into prognostic-score imbalance and differences in forecast errors, clarifying why neither predictive accuracy nor score balance alone guarantees causal identification. The National Supported Work application reveals that stronger pre-treatment covariate balance does not necessarily yield estimates closer to experimental benchmarks, highlighting the practical relevance of prognostic-score comparisons.

title: Minimax-Optimal Static Estimators Under Interference
abstract: We study the problem of estimating the global treatment effect in randomized experiments under interference, where a unit's outcome may depend on the treatment assignments of other units. We adopt a minimax framework, allowing an adversary to select an outcome function from a class of functions that satisfy bounded outcomes and bounded interference. We derive minimax-optimal static estimators that are robust to a wide range of interference structures, parameterized by a scalar $\delta$ controlling the maximum influence of one unit's treatment on another's outcome. Under large interference, we observe two regimes. When the treatment and control groups are equally sized, the minimax-optimal static estimator is the zero estimator. When one of the two groups is larger, the minimax-optimal static estimator is a "half-zero" estimator, in which the outcomes of the smaller group are ignored, and the estimator only considers the outcomes of the larger group.

title: How Green Is Your Manifesto? Scoring Environmental Positions in the 2024 EU Elections with an LLM Panel
abstract: Locating political parties on environmental and climate policy is central to the study of party competition, yet the established instruments, expert surveys and the hand coding of manifestos, are costly, periodic, and slow to extend to new documents. We ask whether a panel of large language models can serve as a cheaper and reproducible alternative. Treating each manifesto as a set of sentences, three models from independent providers score every sentence on two dimensions, environmental protection and climate change, separating a party's position on an issue from the salience it gives it, and the judgments are averaged to the manifesto level. Agreement across the models is retained as a built-in reliability signal. We apply the panel to 41 manifestos from the 2024 European Parliament election, covering Austria, France, Germany, Italy, Spain, and the European party families, and validate it against the 2024 Chapel Hill Expert Survey for the 25 parties with a like-for-like expert benchmark, using the other manifestos as diagnostic cases. The panel recovers the expert ordering of parties with strong rank agreement on both dimensions, while reading them as systematically greener than experts do, a gap we interpret as the distance between manifesto promise and governing record. Inter-model disagreement modestly flags where the instrument errs, and position and salience prove related for environmental protection but independent for climate change. The result is a transparent, low-cost, and multilingual instrument that complements rather than replaces expert and hand-coded approaches; the prompt, code, and manifesto-level results are released openly.

title: Does Calibration Pick the Right Model? Likelihood Evidence from Income Risk
abstract: Quantitative macroeconomics typically disciplines models by matching selected moments. We show how finite-state hidden Markov approximations make likelihood estimation and model selection feasible for nonlinear, non-Gaussian latent processes on short panels, without simulation. We illustrate the method with PSID earnings data. The calibrations that best match moments of earnings dynamics fit complete histories worse than a likelihood-estimated process with a Gaussian persistent component. In a standard saving model, calibrations of one process that fit the targets about equally well imply mean assets that differ by a factor of three. Close agreement with selected moments can leave economic predictions largely undetermined.

title: Randomized Adaptive Sequential Allocation and the Limits of Bounded Exposure to Inferior Treatments
abstract: A clinical trial must learn which treatment is superior while sparing its participants from the inferior one. Kundu et al. 2025 recently showed that a purely deterministic rule, which always assigns the treatment with the larger current sample mean, achieves a strong form of this ethical goal. The smaller allocation count stays almost surely finite and has all moments bounded uniformly in the sample size. Deterministic allocation is, however, predictable, and predictability invites selection bias. We ask whether this bounded-exposure phenomenon survives once the deterministic rule is replaced by a smooth randomized one. We show that it does not. Under any fixed non-degenerate symmetric randomization, both treatments are sampled infinitely often, the adaptive sample means are strongly consistent, and the inferior treatment draws a strictly positive limiting allocation proportion. Consequently, the inferior allocation count grows linearly and its moments are unbounded. We then study annealed randomization, in which the randomization scale cools with the accumulated information, and obtain summability and divergence criteria that separate finite, sublinear, and linear exposure. A forced-exploration variant identifies the superior treatment with probability one while keeping the inferior exposure sublinear, and thereby frees the annealed guarantees from any correct-stabilization event. We also treat normalized multi-treatment rules, ties, indifference zones, unequal variances, general response distributions, and local alternatives. Finally, we develop the post-trial asymptotic inference that each exposure regime permits. The results delineate the trade-off between allocation concealment, persistent exploration, and ethical concentration on the superior treatment.

title: Optimal Online Learning in Bilateral Trade Through Interest
abstract: We consider online learning in bilateral trade on platforms such as Uber, Airbnb, and eBay. In each round, a platform posts a payment to a seller and a price to a buyer, both with private valuations, and observes only whether trade occurs. Its objective is to maximize cumulative gains-from-trade, the sum of the differences between buyers' and sellers' valuations across completed trades. We measure the platform's performance by its regret against the best fixed common price. Financial self-sufficiency motivates global budget balance (Bernasconi et al., 2024), which allows profits from some trades to subsidize others, provided that the final balance is nonnegative. Such financial planning should also account for the time value of money: profits earned earlier can accumulate interest, providing additional funds for future subsidies. Motivated by this observation, we introduce global budget balance with interest, under which a platform starting with no funds can use both trading profits and accrued interest to finance subsidies. For a horizon of $T$ rounds and a fixed exponent $\theta\ge0$, we consider the per-round interest rate $r_T = T^{-\theta}$. We study two classic valuation models, adversarial and correlated i.i.d., and obtain tight bounds on regret against the best fixed common price in both. As the interest rate grows, optimal regret in each model drops from $\tilde\Theta(T^{3/4})$ to $\tilde\Theta(T^{5/7})$. The intermediate rates differ: $\tilde\Theta(T^{3\theta/4})$ for adversarial valuations when $20/21 < \theta < 1$, and $\tilde\Theta(T^{(2\theta+3)/7})$ for correlated i.i.d. valuations when $1 < \theta < 9/8$. Finally, as an extension, we study $\alpha$-regret, with approximation factor $\alpha\ge1$, for adversarial valuations against the best feasible distribution over price pairs, and show that the optimal competitive ratio rises from 2 to 3 as interest strengthens.

title: The precision of fractional factorial designs under randomization
abstract: A regular fraction of a two-level factorial design runs fewer treatment combinations (cells), with more units in each. With the number of units fixed, more units per cell do not by themselves reduce the variance. Averaged over the fractions of one defining contrast subgroup, a fraction's variance is smaller than the full design's by the unit-to-unit variation of the aliased effects, a gain the usual variance estimator misses. Assuming the aliased effects are zero, we propose a full-design estimator that weights the fractions' contrasts by inverse variance. Its estimated variance never exceeds the saturated estimator's. In large samples, it is proportional to the harmonic mean of the fractions' average cell variances, and a fraction's, on average, to the arithmetic mean. We test this assumption, but choosing between the two estimators by the test can lose coverage. The results extend to unequal allocations, and the large-sample results to covariate adjustment.

title: A Compute Center Anyone Can Join: A Peer-to-Peer System for AI Inference
abstract: Today, most people obtain AI inference by buying it from a small number of organizations that run large data centers, while many GPUs owned by individuals and small institutions sit idle for much of the day. Bitcoin showed that strangers can contribute resources under shared rules and receive checkable rewards, but it relies on an asymmetry: proof-of-work is expensive to produce and cheap to verify. Useful inference has no such asymmetry. We propose the Open Inference Market (OIM), which replaces the missing asymmetry with an economic mechanism. A worker delivers a result without knowing whether it will be audited; its unsettled earnings serve as collateral during a challenge window; and confirmed cheating forfeits all of it. We call this principle earnings as collateral. In a simplified model we show three things. The number of audits needed for deterrence is a constant per worker per day, independent of the worker's throughput, so the audited share falls as the network gets busier. A new worker can join with a short period of intensive auditing and a very small bond. And whether the mechanism works at all depends only on the ratio of the audit judge's false-flag rate to its detection rate. Under example parameters, about 0.3 replays per worker per day are enough to make cheating unprofitable for a rational worker. On this basis we lay out a path that hands four powers back to participants one at a time: owning compute, writing history, judging work, and releasing value. A compute center need not be a building; it can be a protocol that anyone can join.

title: Inference for conditional Fr\'echet means via Riemannian Robust Bias Correction
abstract: We develop an intrinsic framework for inference on conditional Fr\'echet means with predictors and responses taking values in finite-dimensional Riemannian manifolds. We derive a second-order expansion of the smoothing bias, represented in the tangent space via the logarithm map, and show that this bias can affect first-order inference. We propose Riemannian robust bias correction (RRBC), which estimates the leading smoothing bias using a local quadratic regression in the response tangent space and corrects the estimator through the exponential map. Our leave-one-out (LOO) covariance estimator uses intrinsic displacements between the full-sample and LOO RRBC estimates, accounting for the variability of the estimated bias correction and its covariance with the local linear estimator. We establish asymptotically valid pointwise confidence sets and simultaneous confidence tubes without undersmoothing. Simulations on spheres and symmetric positive-definite matrices show that RRBC can improve coverage when smoothing bias is nonnegligible. Cardiovascular and ocean-current applications illustrate simultaneous hypothesis testing and inference for smooth functionals.

title: Exploiting Locally Exogeneous Variation in Spatial Data: Linear Regression with Many Small Units
abstract: This article shows how researchers can exploit \textit{locally exogeneous variation} even in the presence of endogeneity, autocorrelation, or spurious correlation. It describes the infill asymptotic properties of generalized least squares estimation with county-level data, Census tract-level data, and similar regional averages, including sufficient conditions for consistency, asymptotic normality, and valid inference.

title: Same Text, Different Filename: Are LLM Judges Biased?
abstract: Yes. In 2026, leading economic journals started using Refine.ink in the technical quality assessment of submissions before publication. I study whether renaming a file changes the perception of the document's quality by LLM judges. I find that three frontier LLMs score the same document differently if you change the document's filename. A person-related label scores higher than no label; there is no consistent preference of own- or rival-based label, nor a penalty for an Asian name, but there is a context-specific bias in assessments whose direction and size vary with both document and label. With LLM-written documents, some self-premium can be detected, but a significant context-dependent label bias remains. Whether to combat it is a question of the costs of evaluation errors.

title: Testing Exogeneity in Nonparametric Instrumental Variable Models
abstract: We propose a test of mean exogeneity in nonparametric instrumental variable models. Under completeness, the null is equivalent to a conditional moment restriction involving the ordinary regression function, so the test avoids estimation of the structural function and its ill-posed inverse problem. We construct a residual-marked empirical process and analyze it through an auxiliary U-process of order two. We derive its limiting distributions under the null and Pitman-type local alternatives of order $n^{-1/2}$, and establish consistency against fixed global alternatives. The analysis reveals a nonparametric estimation effect that invalidates a direct multiplier bootstrap. We propose a computationally simple multiplier bootstrap with a tailor-made indicator correction to account for this effect, and establish its asymptotic validity. Simulations show good size control and power gains over existing methods in the nonparametric designs considered. An application to a wage equation provides evidence against the mean exogeneity of schooling.

title: Learning AI Agents, Market Makers, and Stress in Automated Markets
abstract: Automated markets increasingly route order flow from learning trading agents through automated market makers (AMMs). We model trader archetypes as AI agents defined by their reward functions and analyze the feedback they create on a constant-product AMM. Herd-dominated and arbitrage-dominated markets of equal size have identical return distributions and turnover, so no rule based on volatility, value-at-risk, stress frequency, or volume can tell them apart; yet their stress episodes differ in length by a factor unbounded in the feedback-to-noise ratio $\beta/s$. Serial statistics identify the feedback sign from $\Theta((s/\beta)^2\log(1/\delta))$ observations, and this rate is tight. When agents trade together, profit-seeking agents ride herds rather than lean against them, leading to all-or-nothing participation. Spread-earning market makers restore stability but make liquidity fragile, with discontinuous collapse and hysteresis; maker--taker pricing, not a uniform fee, is the effective instrument.

title: Searching for related contributors to a DNA mixture using single cell analysis
abstract: We propose a staged process for assessing the presence of related individuals in an autosomal STR DNA mixture sample, when it is analysed using a single cell pipeline analysis (as opposed to a bulk mixture analysis). In the absence of a large dataset if single cells from real related people, artificial single cell data is generated by sampling individual locus data taken from single cell dataset of real unrelated people. It is applied to create random admixtures used in a relatedness search for pairs of individuals to illustrate the usefulness of the method.

title: Graph-Based Testing of Conditional Mean Independence with Applications to Large Language Model Evaluation
abstract: We study whether a predictor $X$ provides additional information for predicting a scalar response $Y$ after adjustment for other variables $Z$, formalized by testing $\mathsf{H}_0:\E(Y\mid X,Z)=\E(Y\mid Z)$. Existing methods often require estimating nuisance functions involving $X$, which can be difficult for high-dimensional or structured predictors. We propose a graph-based test that extends the edge count principle to covariate adjustment. It represents $X$ through pairwise dissimilarities, estimates only the baseline regression $\E(Y\mid Z)$, and aggregates products of held-out residuals across graph edges. We develop sample-splitting and two-fold cross-fitting versions. Under regularity conditions, both have standard normal null limits, yielding analytic $p$-values, and are consistent under graph-smooth and graph-rough alternatives. Simulations with vector, image, and network predictors show good size control and power advantages over competing procedures, with cross-fitting improving power across the main alternatives. Applications examine human quality ratings, mathematical error labels, and LLM response preferences. Our method detects associations with quality ratings and an LLM judge's preferences after adjustment for text length and other recorded characteristics.

title: The maximum concentration of results in incomplete round-robin tournaments
abstract: The Herfindahl--Hirschman Index (HHI), a standard measure of market concentration, is widely used to quantify competitive balance in sports tournaments. To enable comparisons over time or across leagues, both its minimum and maximum should be known. The minimum is usually trivial. Our paper provides results on the maximum HHI in incomplete round-robin tournaments, where the set of matches is represented by a regular but not complete undirected graph. We prove that the lower bound of maximum HHI is reached when the tournament consists of independent round-robin groups, while the upper bound of maximum HHI is reached when the set of matches is represented by a bipartite graph. Maximising HHI is computationally difficult even for highly structured graph types corresponding to real-world tournaments, where the teams are partitioned into pots and play the same number of matches against opponents from every pot. The complexity of the problem does not depend on the scoring system or the number of opponents from a pot.

title: Agent-Based Disruption Simulation on an Edge-Level Product-Annotated Supply Network of the Automotive Industry
abstract: Disruptions spread through supply networks when customers cannot replace the products they lose. We ask how portfolio-overlap and product-specific rules for selecting candidate suppliers change cascades when customers search for new suppliers and form new supply edges. From the MarkLines database, we construct a product-annotated network of about 77,000 firms and 197,000 supplier-customer edges in the global automotive industry. We extend an agent-based disruption model with edge-level products, a product-specific substitution rule based on the semantic similarity of product names, and calibrated capacities and inventories. Only 6% of the edges carry observed products. We impute the others and test the imputation against the annotated edges. We run 119,000 simulations. With all other mechanics fixed, the product-specific rule makes the cascades after a hub failure four to five times larger than the portfolio-overlap rule of the original model. Under alternative imputations and similarity thresholds, the factor ranges from 1.2 to 18. Within the simulations, substitutability also shapes which suppliers are critical. Network topology largely determines which firms a shock reaches, and substitutability determines how many of them fail. Of the 50 most damaging suppliers under random disruptions, topology alone identifies 20 and an index that adds product substitutability identifies 32. The index carries over without refitting to a regional scenario modelled on the 2011 Tohoku Earthquake. Supply network risk assessment should account for product-level substitutability and therefore needs product data on supply relationships.

title: Stand-In Effects and Pooling Amplification: Design-Based Tests of Whether Biological World Models Use Actions
abstract: Action-conditioned world models are increasingly trained on data from randomized experiments, and whether their predictions respond to actions is usually checked by replacing or removing the actions and measuring the loss in accuracy. We show that such diagnostics report action effects where there are none: under autocorrelated designs, future actions stand in for history the model does not see, and a better model learns the stand-in better. When the design law is known, a conditional randomization test written as an e-value is valid in finite samples whatever the model, provided the resampler conditions on the full state the design used; resampling from a simpler law reproduces the false effect. We identify a second failure, specific to world models: when many sites share one action sequence (cells in a microscope field, pixels in a frame), the natural pooled score turns small model errors along the action contrast into overwhelming evidence against a true effect. In a pixel world, its median log e-value fell from $-17.3$ to $-6832$ as frames grew from 64 to 4096 pixels, while the oracle's rose. Tempering the score by a design effect estimated on training data changes the bet, not the validity. Our own preregistered analysis of optogenetic ERK experiments failed in exactly this way; a tempered statistic, selected on synthetic data and registered before the data were obtained, then rejected the null on a never-opened field ($E\approx 1.1\times10^{10}$). Every analysis is preregistered, fixed in a dated protocol before it was run, or labelled exploratory, and every reported result is generated from hashed result files.

title: Moment-Orthogonal Quadratic-Envelope E-Processes for Anytime-Valid Location Inference
abstract: E-process confidence sequences for unbounded means typically use a variance bound and a first-order score, leaving skewness and kurtosis unused. We construct a quadratic-envelope e-process from a conditionally centered vector score with a predictable second-moment bound. Under moment information specified independently of the tested stream, it stays positive on unbounded support and gives exact anytime-valid coverage under predictable strategies and fixed mixtures, without score clipping. For a location family with known central moments through order four, the centered observation and its centered square yield an exact confidence sequence whose local width shrinks, relative to a first-order construction, by a factor determined by skewness and kurtosis. At level 5%, the largest null ever-crossing rate was 4.63%; on two zero-inflated-lognormal families median stopping times fell by 36.8-45.8%. When the moments are calibrated on an independent reference sample, a centering-robust factor keeps exact coverage at a closed-form width cost: the median gain was 21.6-30.3% for Gamma(2) and lognormal errors with 10^6 reference observations, and a loss of up to 9.9% with 10^4. On public Fermi gamma-ray detector data with a declared stability margin, it crossed at the current location in 1.8% of 225 windows and stopped 30-35% earlier than the calibrated first-order method.

title: Principled Human-AI Collaboration in Agentic Workflows
abstract: Organizations adopting AI face the challenge of deciding which outputs can be released without human review while meeting the quality standards of human experts. We develop a statistical framework for delegating tasks between experts and black-box generate-verify workflows, in which AI-generated answers are verified and revised over multiple rounds. Before deployment, human experts evaluate selected outputs, and their judgments are used to calibrate the verifier threshold and number of attempts. Our method selects the policy with the highest estimated automation rate among statistically approved candidates, without modifying the generator or verifier. We establish finite-sample control of the error rate among released outputs, characterize the expert evaluations sufficient to attain a target automation rate, and derive a minimax lower bound establishing rate optimality in the quality margin and required confidence. In a MultiHiertt financial question-answering case study, average held-out automation increases from 2.50% to 24.17% as expert evaluations accumulate, while released-output error rates remain around 1.20%. In contrast, heuristics that release answers after consistently high verifier scores either violate the 5% error tolerance or automate at most 1.30% of tasks. Synthetic experiments further examine these theoretical predictions under controlled settings.

title: Social Networks and the Propagation of Household Shocks to Asset Prices
abstract: When can local household disturbances move credit prices? I develop a financially weighted propagation operator on the social network. In a conditional household-intermediary equilibrium, its projection determines the household-demand component of the excess bond premium. Because responses decay at different rates across network patterns and channels, a location's relative financial importance generically changes with the horizon, so no single centrality measure summarizes exposure across horizons. Household measurements recover this projection exactly when they span independently measured demand sensitivities. Empirically, social exposure to storm-damaged counties is negatively associated with spending weeks later in counties outside the recorded footprints. In simulations on the observed network under the model's diffusion law, the operator predicts the propagated credit-premium component of held-out storms with about 30 percent less error than direct social exposure.

title: A Debiased Machine Learning Single-Imputation Framework for Item Nonresponse in Surveys
abstract: Machine-learning methods offer flexible alternatives to parametric models for imputing missing survey values. However, using their predictions in the customary imputed estimator does not automatically yield valid inference. We explain why the error from estimating the regression function can prevent root-$n$ consistency and develop inference for a finite population mean using a cross-fitted augmented inverse-probability-weighted (AIPW) estimator. The analysis combines an imputation model, a sampling design, and a missing-at-random response mechanism, while allowing dependence among sampling indicators. We establish double robustness and show that, under suitable regularity conditions, consistency of both nuisance estimators together with a product-rate condition yields oracle equivalence and asymptotic normality. We also derive consistent variance estimators accounting for sampling and nonresponse. To obtain a completed survey variable, we construct adjusted imputed values that preserve observed responses and whose weighted mean reproduces the AIPW estimate exactly. We further discuss aggregation of nuisance learners and the conditions under which it preserves the prediction rates needed for inference. Simulations show that cross-fitting can substantially reduce undercoverage, but may increase mean squared error when nuisance predictions are inaccurate.

title: The Stability of Data Exchange in Competitive Markets
abstract: We study the stability of data exchange among competing firms. Unlike tangible goods, data is non-rival: sharing it does not deprive the giver of its use. On one hand, competing firms-- often operating as machine-learning-driven predictors that collect observations from a shared environment to solve similar tasks-- can improve their predictive accuracies from pooling data. On the other hand, they compete for market share, which may depend on their relative predictive performance. This raises the central question of this paper: can there be a stable data exchange in such competitive environments? We formalize this via a model of $n$ firms exchanging fractions of their datasets, with predictive performance feeding into market competition. We adopt core stability as our solution concept, accounting for externalities via worst-case responses by non-participating firms. Our main results reveal a sharp contrast driven by demand structure: (i) in fully rational markets, where customers flock entirely to the top-performing firm, a core-stable exchange always exists for any monotone continuous prediction functions; (ii) in partially rational markets with logit-style demand, core-stable exchanges may fail to exist-and even approximate cores can be empty. Our impossibility results suggest that internal profit-sharing within coalitions can restore stability in partially rational markets. We formalize this intuition by showing that when co-operating coalitions equally redistribute market-share revenues among members, a core-stable data exchange exists. Finally, we propose a natural exchange dynamic and demonstrate empirically that it converges to a core-stable data exchange in fully rational markets on simulated instances derived from real datasets.

title: Transport for Conditional Sampling: Foundations and Applications
abstract: Conditional sampling is central to Bayesian inference, generative modeling, and causal inference: given a joint law for random variables $X$ and $Y$ and an observation $Y=y$, one seeks to sample from the conditional law of $X\mid Y=y$. Even when the joint distribution is accurately represented, this task can be computationally difficult as it may require evaluating intractable normalizing constants or solving a new inference problem for each observation. Measure transport provides an approach to this problem by identifying a map with triangular structure that directly pushes forward a reference to the conditional of a joint distribution for any observation. This article reviews the theoretical, methodological, and algorithmic foundations of triangular transports, with the Knothe-Rosenblatt rearrangement as a canonical construction. We discuss methods for estimating triangular maps from finite samples, as well as their use in simulation-based inference and causal inference. While our primary aim is to review existing formulations, we also present new ideas and open questions for conditional sampling using transport.

title: Longest-Queue Policies in Dynamic Matching with Abandonments
abstract: We study a dynamic two-way matching market in which agents of heterogeneous types arrive over time, wait to be matched according to a compatibility network, and abandon the system if their random patience expires. The decision maker collects match rewards and pays holding and abandonment costs, and seeks to maximize the expected net value over a finite horizon. We evaluate policies by their approximation ratio against a fluid benchmark, the optimal value of a linear-programming relaxation that upper bounds the expected net value of every policy. Under a general position gap (GPG) condition, which requires the unique optimal dual solution of this linear program to remain optimal under small perturbations of the arrival rates, we propose a longest-queue policy. The policy first uses this dual solution to identify a set of good match types and a set of critical agent types. Upon each arrival, it considers only good matches and matches the arrival to the critical partner with the longest queue subject to availabilities. In the high-volume regime, in which arrival rates are scaled by s, we prove that the policy attains an approximation ratio of at least 1-O(1/s) at every scale s >= 1 and every horizon T >= 1, so the ratio tends to 1 as s goes to infinity.

title: The Costs and Benefits of Leveraged ETFs
abstract: We study the costs and benefits of leveraged ETFs (LETFs), focusing on five determinants of performance: volatility drag, fees, financing costs, product launches, and market timing. Long broad-equity-index LETFs generated more than 100 billion US dollars in investor gains, including over 40 billion US dollars relative to counterfactual investments in the underlying assets, due to modest structural headwinds and rising markets. Single-stock LETFs, however, are launched on stocks near the top of the volatility and past-return distributions. This caters to retail demand for lottery-like payoffs, but it also creates larger volatility drag, higher financing costs, and greater exposure to losses from poor market timing.

title: Measurement Error and Nonlinear Confounding: Structural Equation Modeling Versus Double Machine Learning
abstract: A latent confounder measured by fallible indicators can be adjusted for with structural equation modeling (SEM), which corrects measurement error but requires a specified functional form, or with double machine learning (DML), which learns the form but ignores measurement error. We derive both population biases and the crossover reliability, the composite reliability above which DML with the indicators or their mean as inputs is less biased than linear SEM; it depends on the nonlinear share of confounding and falls when covariates predict the confounder. A 46-condition Monte Carlo study confirmed both biases and the predicted ordering. With gradient boosting, learning the conditional means raised the DML bias by up to 0.05 and moved the finite-sample crossover upward. A quadratic SEM was unbiased when its form was correct and removed two thirds of the linear-SEM bias under a saturating nonlinearity but little of it under a cubic one.

title: Sentiment sensing: comparative analysis of multilingual sentiment dynamics
abstract: Cross-country sentiment analysis faces three fundamental challenges: language-specific biases distort comparisons, compositional data constraints invalidate standard statistics and temporal dynamics lack rigorous testing frameworks. We introduce sentiment sensing, a framework that addresses these gaps through integrated statistical methods. By combining compositional data analysis, functional data methods, and non-parametric inference, sentiment sensing enables valid multilingual comparisons and statistically defensible detection of sentiment shifts. Our framework has been tested in two case studies, analyzing news articles from the 27 countries of the European Union on the topics of energy and artificial intelligence. Sentiment sensing focuses on multilingual sentiment analysis enabling rigorous comparative science.

title: Optimal Certified Multiple Testing with E-values
abstract: We study randomized multiple testing with e-values under arbitrary dependence and introduce a conditional certification constraint: Given the observed evidence, each coordinate's expected rejection certificate must not exceed its e-value. Existing randomized e-BH improvements satisfy this constraint but have no established optimality guarantee. We prove that the maximum conditional inclusion probability for hypothesis $i$, given e-values~$x$, is $1 \wedge (\alpha / K) \sum_j \min(x_i, x_j)$, and construct one rule attaining these bounds simultaneously. The rule uses a single independent uniform variable, rejects a prefix of the ordered e-values, and has a unique conditional rejection-set law among rules attaining all the bounds. It therefore maximizes every nonnegative weighted sum of inclusion probabilities, including expected true discoveries under any truth configuration. Under a shared uniform draw, its rejection set contains those of e-BH and U-eBH. The construction extends to BY-calibrated p-values, and simulations under positive and negative dependence show power gains over existing randomized procedures.

title: Floods and the Duplication of Production: Evidence from the Global Car Industry
abstract: Floods are becoming more frequent and can disrupt global supply chains. We study how multinational car makers adapt vehicle and key parts production to flood risk, and how their choices interact with insurance and public flood defences. Using plant-level data and a manually verified flood record in a staggered difference-in-differences design, we find that car makers duplicate production rather than move it away from flooded plants. Even more than five years after a flood, an engine is 19 percentage points more likely to be made in two or more plants, usually abroad and for cars assembled nearby, while the flooded plant's output shows no persistent decline beyond a temporary loss in the flood year. Firms duplicate only where adjustment costs are low, i.e. when a plant of theirs abroad already makes the same engine family. Flooded vehicle model versions are duplicated only temporarily, and transmission programs are not duplicated. Suggestive evidence that firms duplicate more where insurance is likely expensive and plants lack flood defences points to substitution between redundancy, insurance and public protection.

title: Accuracy Is Not Risk: Why Medical AI Should Not Report Only Its Most Likely Label
abstract: Background. Many medical AI models are trained to reproduce a single reference label and hand the most likely label to the next step in a clinical workflow. A classifier can select that label correctly while providing an inadequate summary for estimating downstream risk. Methods. We use Jeffrey's rule of conditioning to specify when probabilities over intermediate states, such as diagnoses or imaging categories, can be carried forward to an outcome risk. We separate two errors of reporting only the most likely label, discarding the probability of the other states and applying the risk of patients who have the leading diagnosis to a patient who only probably has it. We also give conditions under which the label and the full distribution lead to the same decision, and we propose guardrails for device developers, regulatory reviewers, and health insurers. Results. In a hypothetical chest-pain differential, reporting only the benign leading diagnosis greatly understates the patient's risk of death or cardiac arrest, so a patient who warrants evaluation could be discharged or denied imaging. In a hypothetical BI-RADS example, the most likely category is "probably benign," yet the propagated malignancy risk exceeds the ceiling that defines that category. Conclusions. A predicted label is not an observed state, and a calibrated classifier is not automatically a valid outcome model. Clinical and insurance coverage decisions should rest on the patient's outcome risk, judged against a threshold justified by the consequences of acting and not acting. Developers should state what each model output means and check that every step between the model and the decision preserves the patient's risk.

title: An analytical model to explain under which conditions home batteries create new load peaks in the local grid
abstract: Simulation studies find that price-responsive home batteries and electric vehicles create new load peaks in low-voltage grids; with endogenous wholesale prices most of these peaks disappear. This paper explains both findings with an analytical model of the coincident peak at the transformer. The model is algebraic and solved in closed form, so the parameters that determine whether a new peak emerges and how large it becomes can be identified; they are few. The peak is the background load in the critical hour plus the charging of the local fleet. Under exogenous prices the charging equals the rated power of the fleet. Under endogenous prices the national fleet fills the trough of residual load until the price is flat; the depth of the fill follows from an energy balance in which the price function does not appear. For a V-shaped trough the local charging peak is the share of the grid in national flexibility times the square root of flank gradient times national flexibility. Rated power, price level, network charge and market size do not enter. The model reproduces simulated peaks for a German case within a few percent.

title: Model-Based Co-Clustering for Censored Data
abstract: Co-clustering jointly partitions the rows and columns of a data matrix. Standard co-clustering methods for continuous data typically assume that entries are observed exactly. Matrices with censored entries, such as assay measurements below a detection limit, are therefore commonly completed by substitution or imputation before co-clustering. Since the completed values are treated as exact, the estimated block means and partitions depend on the completion rule. We propose the censored Gaussian latent block model (CGLBM), in which each censored entry contributes the probability of its reported interval. We establish identifiability under a known Type I censoring design. Approximate standard errors for the block means follow from the Fisher information under censoring. CGLBM is fitted by a generalized expectation--maximization algorithm, and its row and column class numbers are selected by a BIC approximation to the integrated classification likelihood. In simulation studies, boundary substitution and truncated normal imputation attenuate the contrasts between block means, whereas the partition recovery of multiple imputation drops the most under heavy censoring. CGLBM preserves the contrasts, and its partition recovery drops the least. The method is implemented in the R package CGLBM.

title: How Much Can Approximate Equilibria Change the Social Cost of Selfish Routing?
abstract: We study approximate Nash equilibria in nonatomic congestion games, with the goal of understanding how much the social cost can change when the equilibrium condition is relaxed. We consider $\epsilon$-approximate Nash equilibria ($\epsilon$-NE), in which each player uses a strategy whose cost is at most $1 + \epsilon$ times the minimum available cost. We compare the social costs of $\epsilon$-NE and exact Nash equilibria. This lets us quantify, for example, how much a navigation app can reduce total travel time when drivers tolerate routes slightly slower than the fastest available route. For degree-$d$ polynomial latencies in both general nonatomic congestion games and single-commodity routing games on series-parallel networks, we give tight lower and upper bounds on the relative change in social cost from an exact Nash equilibrium to any $\epsilon$-NE, with matching instances for every $\epsilon$. For small $\epsilon$, the largest possible relative reduction and increase in general congestion games are both $\Theta(\sqrt{d\epsilon})$, independently of the number of resources and populations. In contrast, on series-parallel networks of depth $h$, the largest possible relative reduction is $\Theta(h\epsilon)$, while the largest possible relative increase is known to be $\epsilon$. For the classes of games we study, these results give a tight and quantitative characterization of the possible changes in social cost and establish a separation between general and series-parallel networks.

title: Learning about Markets from Models: Evidence from an AI Hiring Platform
abstract: Machine learning models are increasingly used to not only inform, but make decisions. Sometimes platforms add value by pooling data across contexts to improve models' decision making---but when the optimal decision differs by context, pooling may not increase accuracy. We argue that a platform storing starkly distinct models across contexts nevertheless captures a model comparison externality. Together, these models reflect how decision makers respond differently to the same data in the current equilibrium. Policymakers can use this differentiation to prioritize interventions; firms can learn how they are already differentiated from competitors to focus future investments. Our evidence comes from an AI hiring platform used by large employers of low-skill workers. The platform uses a standardized psychometric assessment to create firm-specific models estimating each application's retention likelihood at that firm. Each firm's model is highly predictive for itself but no better than chance at other firms. We use these models to create a firm-application matrix: each firm scores each application, not only the ones it receives. An application's improved retention likelihood if submitted to a different firm is highly heterogeneous based on traits. Further, these gains are due to two distinct mechanisms. Finally, firms value traits differently even in this low skill market: they disagree about whether important traits improve or worsen retention at the margin. These insights are only possible when a platform can access both the full application pool and each firm-specific model. We explain the value of these insights to firms, policymakers, and platforms.

title: Geodesics and intrinsic statistics of isolated connections in Hermitian positive-definite matrices
authors: Ronald Garc\'ia Reyes and Pedro Antonio Vald\'es-Sosa
abstract: Quantifying change in a single covariance, coherence or spectral connection requires a distance that respects the positive-definiteness constraint and holds the surrounding entries fixed. We characterize the Riemannian geometry induced by the affine-invariant metric when one conjugate off-diagonal pair of a Hermitian positive-definite matrix varies under this constraint. A fixed Schur congruence maps the admissible set to an open complex disk and reduces its metric to a two-dimensional form independent of the ambient matrix dimension. The disk is complete, with Gaussian curvature in $(-1/4,0]$, and has unique minimizing geodesics and globally defined logarithms. Its intrinsic distance strictly exceeds the ambient affine-invariant distance between distinct points. Conservation of angular momentum reduces the geodesic boundary-value problem to a single scalar equation with elementary angular and length integrals, enabling distance and logarithm evaluation without shooting. For a declared reference distribution with a finite second intrinsic moment, we establish a unique Fr\'echet centre and consistency of its empirical estimate, together with a sandwich central limit theorem under the stated regularity conditions. Tangent covariance standardization yields moment identities, and exchangeable rank calibration supplies finite-sample score guarantees. These results provide a geometric and statistical framework for isolated connections on a fixed complement, with explicit limits on extension to varying complements.

title: A model-based adaptive sampling framework for infectious disease surveillance
abstract: Longitudinal surveillance must choose each round's sampling design before the next observations arrive. Fixed sample-size rules treat each round as an isolated cross-sectional survey and ignore the evolving uncertainty in the epidemic process, which changes as transmission, vaccination, interventions, variants, and behavior change. We present a model-based adaptive sampling framework for choosing the next-round design. A state-space model represents the epidemic process and maps latent states to surveillance estimands. A statistical filter calibrates the model as observations arrive, propagating uncertainty in latent states, time-varying parameters, stochastic dynamics, and sampling noise. A Bayesian assurance criterion converts the one-step-ahead predictive distribution into the minimum-cost design likely to achieve a target posterior credible-interval width. We evaluated the framework in two simulations and in a retrospective case study of SARS-CoV-2 serosurveillance among Canadian blood donors in four regions, replaying the series with each week's specimens subsampled to the selected design. In simulations, the policy increased sampling effort during an anticipated high-variance period, and the share of intervals meeting the width target (0.970) agreed with validated assurance (0.974). After an unanticipated change in transmission rate, validated assurance stayed at 0.960 while the share meeting the target fell to 0.894 (95% Monte Carlo interval 0.869 to 0.919) in the transition window. Sampling effort rose while the filter relearned the transmission rate, then fell. In the case study, recommended sample sizes tracked the one-step predictive uncertainty and were largest during the Omicron wave, and the 90% filtering interval had width at most 0.10 in 94% of region-rounds with specimens. The modular framework extends to other pathogens, data streams, and surveillance objectives.

title: Recommendations with Costly Verification
abstract: A recommender faces consumers who can verify recommendations, but differ in their attention costs or in the salience of their choice of adoption. We characterize the conditions under which a technology that increases transparency by lowering the cost of verifying a product's quality will increase or decrease false recommendations. Without commitment, reducing verification costs never increases false recommendations, but when the recommender can commit to a policy, transparency can worsen both the quality of recommendations and consumer welfare. The necessary and sufficient condition is that the log-elasticity of the distribution of consumer cost types is decreasing. It can hold when the distribution is sufficiently fat-tailed, or when it mixes sophisticated and naive consumers. Our results can be applied to platform-recommended listings, security ratings, and audits.

title: Organizing Intelligence
abstract: When will advances in AI lead to economic transformation? We develop a model of how intelligence, the ability to achieve goals, matters for organizations, the key unit of economic production. Agents (human or AI) with multidimensional capabilities sort endogenously into competing firms. A firm's productivity depends on its agents' capabilities; we distinguish competence, which shifts productivity levels, from coordination, which governs how productivity scales with size. Two differences between AI and humans drive transformation: AI expertise is reproducible while humans' are in fixed supply, and AIs may not face the same human limits on coordination. We analyze how equilibrium market structure, productivity, employment, and wages evolve as AI capabilities improve. When AI is more capable than the average human, organizations of complementary humans can nonetheless outperform AI. Increases in AI competence can change the composition of workers within firms and decrease firm size. As AI coordination improves, however, this can break the Coasean ceiling on firm size and the market structure undergoes a phase transition toward large, concentrated AI-heavy firms. Changes in human employment are gradual when AI displaces workers within mixed human-AI firms, or sudden when AI firms outcompete human firms. We decompose wage changes into a technology effect, which changes the value of humans within existing firms, and a reorganization effect as firms adjust size and composition. Reorganization can reverse the technology effect on wages.

title: Selective inference for pruned interaction trees with known unequal variances in randomized trials
abstract: Interaction trees reuse outcomes to discover treatment-effect heterogeneity, complicating inference after growth and pruning. We develop selective inference for generalized least-squares (GLS) interaction trees with a common covariate basis and known unequal variances. Under a conditional Gaussian model with positive diagonal covariance, weighted orthogonality reduces survival under additive fixed-penalty pruning to one quadratic inequality supplementing the growth event. This yields exact finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals, with retained-path and complete-tree inference agreeing on compatible sections. Under causal identification and a correct reference prognosis, the pruning-invariant GLS target is a signed finite-design weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects. Simulations at $n=100,200,400,800$ and maximum depths one to three search all adjacent-observation midpoints, support calibration and demonstrate over-rejection when pruning survival is omitted. Compared with a 50:50 honest procedure, full-data learning improves reference-split recovery in some small-sample settings. Root-level median intervals can be shorter, while deep-node intervals and upper tails can be much wider; these comparisons concern each procedure's selected targets. Estimating a common scale with the variance ratio fixed produces modest changes in Selective coverage in the settings examined, without extending the exact guarantee. An exploratory ACTG 175 analysis provides a working-model illustration with estimated arm variances.

title: A Kernel-Based Test for Multi-Way Conditional Independence
abstract: Conditional independence involving more than two variables, or multi-way conditional independence, is a fundamental probabilistic structure useful in many areas of statistical research, including latent-variable and graphical models. However, most existing works focus on pairwise conditional independence. To address this gap, we propose a kernel-based test of multi-way conditional independence. Specifically, we characterize this hypothesis through the simultaneous vanishing of a vector of conditional cross-covariance operators and construct a test statistic based on the norm of the vector of their estimators. We derive the statistic's asymptotic distributions under the null hypothesis and local alternatives. As a related methodological contribution, we also develop a test of multi-way unconditional independence and provide a procedure for its implementation. An application to RNA data illustrates the method's use in genomics.

title: Contracting for Experimentation with Private Findings
abstract: A principal hires an agent to work on a project of unknown quality. Success is contractible, but before it occurs, the agent may privately obtain a favorable finding. For example, a scientist developing a drug may observe a promising microscope reading. An informed agent may conceal the finding; an uninformed agent may fake one. The agent's private information could guide both the project's duration and his pay. Yet I show that an optimal contract pays only success bonuses tied to time, not reported findings, consistent with time-based payment schedules often used in research funding. Dynamically arriving private information drives this simplicity: the agent can conceal good news to retain higher bonuses, so deterring concealment limits pay differences across report histories. Bonuses are high and rising in a research stage that induces learning, then fall to a low, constant level in a development stage where only an informed agent continues working. Rising bonuses reflect a novel force: rents from private learning motivate effort but shrink as fewer research periods remain.

title: Unlikely likelihoods: likelihood analysis for the triangular and random histogram models
abstract: This paper concerns certain parametric models for densities on the unit interval which lead to nonsmooth and nonregular likelihood functions. (i) The first is the simple triangular model on the unit interval, characterised by a density linearly increasing from zero to the mode position $\theta$ and then linearly decreasing to zero from the mode to one. With data from this model the likelihood function is a sum of individually log-convex terms, and with the derivative having discontinuities at each data point. (ii) The second is the one-parameter two-box density which is flat on $[0,\theta]$ and $(\theta,1]$, with $\theta$ the median. The likelihood has jumps at each datapoint. Here the maximum likelihood estimator is sharper than usual, with convergence in distribution of $n(\hat\theta-\theta)$ to a nonnormal limit. We also study the $k$-box extension of this model, with density being flat on $k$ boxes determined by $k$ quantiles. (iii) This second model is extended to the two-parameter two-box model, with areas $\gamma$ and $1-\gamma$ for boxes $[0,\theta]$ and $(\theta,1]$. Again the likelihood is nonregular, and the maximum likelihood estimators exhibit different rates of convergence for the breakpoints and the density values. The model generalises to the $2(k-1)$ parameter density piecewise flat over $k$ boxes. For each of these models we tend to the delicate task of sorting out the large-sample behaviour of the log-likelihoods, then leading to precise and partly nonstandard limit distributions for the maximum likelihood and Bayes estimators.

title: Second-Order Least Squares Method for Statistical Inference in Linear Models with Asymmetric Errors
abstract: In a linear regression model with normal random errors, the ordinary least squares estimator is the most efficient estimator. However, when the random errors have an asymmetric distribution, a more efficient estimator can be constructed using the higher moments of the data. In this paper, we use the second-order least squares method to obtain more accurate asymptotic confidence intervals and more powerful hypothesis tests in linear models. We also develop an efficient and stable numerical algorithm to calculate the proposed estimator. Our extensive simulation studies demonstrate the advantages of the proposed method. Two real data examples are presented.

title: Optimal Learning in Fairness-Aware Contextual Bandits
abstract: Mitigating unfair disparities in sequential decision-making is a growing concern in machine learning. We study contextual bandits under a global covariate-based Lipschitz fairness constraint, pioneered by \cite{dwork2012fairness}, requiring individuals with similar contexts to receive similar action distributions. We show that this constraint induces a randomisation region near the decision boundary and explicitly quantify the population level cost of fairness. We further establish a canonical representation of the optimal fair policy, which reduces the fair policy design to a lower-dimensional boundary optimisation problem. We develop a lazy fair greedy algorithm that exploits fairness-induced covariate diversity under continuous contexts, with policy updates computed via finite-dimensional linear programming. For general context distributions, including discrete and mixed contexts, we propose a lazy polyhedral upper confidence bound (UCB) algorithm, whose optimistic optimisation reduces to finitely many linear programs over confidence-set vertices. Both methods satisfy fairness at every round and achieve regret of order $O(\sqrt{T} + T^{(d-2)/(d-1)}{\indc\{d\geq 4\}})$ up to poly-logarithmic factors, where $d$ is the dimension of the contexts. A matching minimax lower bound for $\ell_1$-based fairness establishes optimality, and reveals an unavoidable nonparametric cost of learning the decision boundary, which dominates the parametric learning cost when $d \geq 4$. Experiments on synthetic and real data support our theoretical findings and demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our methods.

title: High-Frequency Estimation of the Leverage Effect under Rough Volatility with Microstructure Noise
abstract: This paper develops feasible high-frequency inference for the leverage effect when the spot variance follows rough Volterra dynamics, leverage loadings depend on endogenous rough states, and observed prices may be contaminated by microstructure noise. We define an integrated leverage parameter through a scaled covariation between log prices and spot variance that accounts for their different local fluctuation scales. The scaled realized covariation admits a stable functional central limit theorem with an explicit pathwise centering correction arising from within-interval variation in the leverage loading. A loading regularity condition renders this correction asymptotically negligible, and we verify the condition for direct Volterra loadings and for smooth functions of closed rough states for every Hurst index below one half. We construct a block-based estimator with an exact finite-window correction for the leading proportional bias, together with a nonnegative single-scale estimator of its asymptotic variance. Pre-averaging extends feasible inference to observations with independent and identically distributed microstructure noise. Simulations under the rough Heston model demonstrate accurate finite-sample calibration with and without noise. An empirical application to fifteen years of one-second data on nine U.S. equities and ETFs finds negative median leverage estimates for every asset at weekly and monthly horizons.

title: A Bayesian Magnitude-Composition Model for Tree-Size Distributions and Stand-Tables
authors: Andrew O. Finley and Malcolm S. Itter and Arthur Spitta and Arne Nothdurft
abstract: Sparse forest inventories often provide too few plots to estimate species-specific tree-size distributions for individual stands. We develop a general Bayesian magnitude-composition model that separates overall abundance from its allocation among categories. A negative-binomial model describes total counts, while multinomial models describe how those counts are allocated among categories. In forest inventory, this construction allocates trees among species and then size classes within species, without imposing a parametric form on the tree-size distribution. Covariates inform both abundance and composition. Shared latent factors represent residual spatial and group-level dependence among categories using relatively few processes, while smoothing priors on regression coefficients borrow information across neighboring size classes. Nearest-neighbor Gaussian processes support efficient spatial computation.
