Joint posterior prediction and area-weighted aggregation yield stand-tables---tree densities by species and size class---and derived measures such as size-class diversity, with associated uncertainty. Simulations show small estimation errors and near-nominal predictive-interval coverage for forest and stand summaries. An application combining field plots and light detection and ranging (LiDAR) covariates illustrates estimation of species-specific distributions of diameter at breast height and size-class diversity in sampled and unsampled stands.

title: Deformed Q-learning for High-Dimensional Dynamic Treatment Regimes
abstract: In high-dimensional dynamic treatment regimes, nonlinear terminal outcome models complicate upstream conditional-mean modeling and inference based on recursively estimated continuation values. We introduce a Deformed Q-learning procedure for general action spaces that accommodates a terminal-stage GLM, random designs, conditional heteroscedasticity, and fine-grained action discretization. The procedure changes the recursive criterion by propagating the terminal deformed optimal Q-function through sparse block-wise linear conditional-mean models. Under the stated models and regularity conditions, we establish consistent and asymptotically normal estimators, accounting for downstream estimation uncertainty in inference for optimal Q-values, deformed optimal Q-values, and their contrasts. We bound population regret relative to the original terminal mean-outcome objective without explicit stage-wise accumulation. Estimation and inference also extend to a growing number of stages under conditions uniform across stages. Simulation studies demonstrate accurate estimation and variable selection. In an empirical application to sepsis management using the MIMIC-III database, the proposed framework supports stage-specific value inference, while an auxiliary action-alignment analysis provides an exploratory signal that early-stage concordance with the learned recommendation may be associated with improved survival.

title: Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality
authors: Jiahe Li and Jerome P. Reiter
abstract: The mean log deviation and the Theil index are two widely used measures of income inequality. The organization releasing these measures may be obligated to protect the confidentiality of the individual incomes used in the computations. In particular, the organization may wish to release versions of these measures with formal guarantees of privacy. The organization could do so by satisfying differential privacy; however, typical applications of differentially private algorithms are likely to add so much noise to the measures that they become unusable. We present differentially private algorithms for these indices with reasonable error properties. The algorithms rely on computing or approximating bounds on the smooth sensitivity, that is, the maximum absolute amount the inequality measures change when replacing any subset of the $n$ incomes in the reported data with arbitrarily chosen feasible values. For the mean log deviation, the algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time. For the Theil index, the algorithm runs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We illustrate the performance of each differentially private algorithm using individual-level and household-level income data from the Current Population Survey. We also examine repeated sampling properties of the algorithms using artificially generated data. The empirical results indicate when these differentially private algorithms can be expected to provide accurate estimates and when they are likely to introduce too much noise.

title: Finite-Sample Calibration and Power Benchmarks in Two-Sample Random-Integration Tests
abstract: In high-dimensional two-group studies, a supplied variable set can be used directly or to learn a projection. We study how much attainable power these choices retain at fixed observation and calibration budgets. For complete unbiased random-integration statistics under Gaussian common shape, a fixed-spectrum comparison orders direction-wise power and gives an explicit criterion balancing an oracle advantage against learning loss. Joint regeneration controls level for a specified learner with unknown diagonal shape. A paired construction permits observation reuse and finite-reference calibration of fitted scores and menus. In the paired diagonal experiment, an invariant sparse likelihood-ratio benchmark provides an attainable efficiency target. Finite-amplitude bounds connect a classical bounded quadratic to this target; conditioning on the coordinate maximum yields informative complementary bounds at moderate and strong signals. Both comparisons include finite reference budgets, and null-only simulations certify local comparisons with specified fitted rules. Equal-budget experiments and a leukemia application compare aggregation, projection and fitted quadratic scores. For correlated paired data, classical sign randomization supplies a separate calibration under central symmetry. The efficiency guarantees apply to the stated experiments and signal classes; general small-budget shape efficiency and adaptation to unknown signal allocation remain open.

title: Power-optimal allocation in multi-arm cluster randomized trials
authors: Muneeb Ahmad Wani and Satya Prakash Singh
abstract: This paper discusses a power-based framework for optimal allocation in multi-arm cluster randomized trials with continuous or binary outcomes, allowing cluster sizes and within-cluster correlations to differ across treatment groups. We consider optimal cluster allocation with prespecified cluster sizes as well as joint optimization of cluster allocations and sizes. Using generalized estimating equations to account for correlated outcomes and a quasi-score test to assess treatment homogeneity, we derive locally optimal designs, which depend on specified parameter values. Since locally optimal designs can be highly sensitive to changes in the parameter values, we also propose maximin designs, which maximize the minimum power over a prescribed parameter space and provide robust allocations under parameter uncertainty. We analytically characterize the maximin designs and the least favorable configurations of treatment means and provide procedures for determining the sample size required to attain a target power. Applications to the WASH Benefits Bangladesh and SCORE trials illustrate gains in calculated power and reductions in the required sample size relative to the original trial designs.

title: Causal Record Linkage
abstract: Combining observations from multiple data sources creates a valuable resource for research. In causal inference, record linkage methods grant researchers access to the covariates needed for unbiased estimation and offer the means to explore (long-term) outcomes. This paper examines how record linkage conflicts with the assumptions required for identifying causal effects. Our investigation reveals that linkage errors primarily threaten consistency in the causal framework, leading to attenuation bias in the inference due to discrepancies in the linked data. In attempting to address this bias by being more stringent on the linkage, sampling bias inadvertently emerges from a covariate shift between the baseline and the linked samples, as profiles with more distinctive information are more likely to be recovered. Despite these challenges, we identify settings in which record linkage and causal inference can be soundly combined, and show how the effect estimated on linked data can be generalised, with linkage decisions informed accordingly. We further identify when existing and novel solutions support valid causal inference on linked data, and when inference should instead be treated with caution or even abandoned. We illustrate the challenges raised and the potential solutions using real data from a study of women's health and a simulation study.

title: Pricing Today, Shaping Tomorrow: Contextual Dynamic Pricing in Purchase-Driven Evolving Systems
abstract: Across diverse markets, it is important for firms to balance attracting customers with managing operational conditions, such as workloads and delivery times. Dynamic pricing plays a central role in this tradeoff, as the orders generated today can change the conditions faced by future customers. We develop a novel framework for contextual dynamic pricing with an observed shared state and unknown purchase-driven transitions. The valuation model allows unknown mean functions of customer covariates and state, unknown state-specific scales and a common unknown standardized noise distribution. We propose Shadow-Adjusted Pricing in Evolving Systems (SHAPE), which incorporates a purchase's future revenue consequences into current pricing. Purchase-shadow adjustment and scale standardization reveal a common one-dimensional oracle price map across states, allowing SHAPE to retain its pricing history across value updates without repeating coarse exploration. The same active sales records support price-map learning and joint updates of continuation values and purchase shadows, without fitting the noise distribution or full transition matrices. To support this reuse under purchase-driven feedback, we establish pricing guarantees for history-dependent inputs and stability bounds for the joint updates. Under regularity, coverage and design conditions, we obtain sublinear expected regret against a finite-horizon dynamic oracle for linear, H\"older and sparse linear mean models. For affine valuations at fixed state and feature dimensions, SHAPE matches the static semiparametric minimax time exponent up to logarithmic factors for every fixed noise-tail smoothness order $\beta\ge2$. Numerical experiments further demonstrate the appealing performance of SHAPE.

title: Certified computation of Buehler confidence limits for system reliability
abstract: Component tests can support a lower confidence limit for a system that has not been tested as a whole, but numerical optimization can compromise its coverage. A feasible point in the minimization defining a Buehler limit gives an upper bound on that limit; reporting it can therefore overstate reliability. We develop a computation that maintains lower and upper bounds on the ideal endpoint for a prescribed ordering. Bounds over entire parameter regions justify the reported lower endpoint at every completed checkpoint, including under adaptive stopping and selection among runs. Separate refinement conditions establish convergence, and an explicit error allocation accounts for simulated tail probabilities and confidence-region localization. The theory retains nuisance and dependence parameters in the observation model. Monotone corner bounds give the implemented specialization for scalar and two-component binomial systems; Bernstein and probability-distance bounds provide further theoretical constructions. Four benchmark problems reach a certified width of $10^{-5}$ under each of four search strategies. Additional stochastic candidates increase cost without reducing subdivisions, whereas complete sample-space enumeration verifies the implemented coverage at three parameter vectors. For the all-success example, the certified lower limit is $0.68128$, compared with $0.41738$ from Bonferroni-adjusted component limits.

title: von Neumann-Morgenstern stable sets in job matching problems
abstract: We show that a von Neumann-Morgenstern (vNM) stable set generically exists in the many-to-one job-matching model. Unlike the core, which can be empty in this model, a vNM stable set exists whenever there is a unique efficient matching: the set of all individually rational (IR) and efficient outcomes form a vNM stable set. If an economy has multiple efficient matchings, a vNM stable set may not exist. If the vNM stable sets are required to be rich in a certain sense, then such a rich vNM stable set exists if and only if the set of efficient matchings is essentially unique, and the set of all efficient and IR outcomes forms the unique rich vNM stable set.

title: Estimating Average Treatment Effects with Projected Instrumental Variables
abstract: In this paper, we develop a projected instrumental variable framework that relaxes conventional assumptions for causal identification with instrumental variables. Building on the interpretation of conditional expectation as an orthogonal projection in a Hilbert space, the framework replaces the conditional expectation operator with a general projection operator. We provide an alternative inverse problem formulation based on the Riesz representation. Drawing on semiparametric efficiency theory, we further develop debiased and adaptive machine learning methods for estimation and inference. The proposed framework connects invalid instrumental variables to instrumented difference-in-differences. We also examine invalid projected instrumental variables and discuss their relationship to existing methods. Simulation studies and real data analysis demonstrate that the proposed methods perform favorably compared with existing approaches.

title: Nonnegativity Shapes Predictive Uncertainty: Complementary Model Fits and Quantile Construction
abstract: Knowing that a response cannot be negative can inform predictive uncertainty, including extreme upper quantiles. This knowledge matters especially when a black-box system returns long vector responses at few covariate settings, leaving large uncertainty across many entries. We develop a framework that assembles predictive distributions feature by feature from distributional fits that incorporate nonnegativity, optionally around any given mean predictor. The fits come from a latent factor model that represents response intensity through nonnegative patterns whose amplitudes follow rectified Gaussian processes over covariates. A variational algorithm jointly learns the factorization and the latent posterior. Varying a conditional-dispersion parameter yields a spectrum of fits that show complementary strengths in estimating distributional shape features. An orthogonal quantile expansion motivates using L-moments or their ratios as features. We select a fit separately for each using scores computable from a single validation observation per entry, then assemble the selected estimates through the expansion. In simulations, this construction reduces extreme upper-quantile errors by 17-22% relative to the respective best single fit, despite the mode-seeking tendency of our variational inference. In a streamflow demonstration across agricultural catchments, using an external point simulation to supply the mean reduces miss rates of rare shortage by 86-91%.

title: When Does $N$ Buy Precision? Heterogeneous Responses to Aggregate Shocks in Micro Panels
abstract: Panel local projections (panel LPs), valued for their flexibility and robustness, are widely used to estimate heterogeneous responses to aggregate shocks from micro data. This paper, however, highlights the potential of panel vector autoregressions (panel VARs) and characterizes the trade-off between the efficiency of panel VARs and the robustness of panel LPs. In contrast to existing results in the time-series literature, we show that under correct specification, panel VAR estimators of the heterogeneous responses converge at rate $(NT)^{-1/2}$, whereas panel LP estimators converge at rate $T^{-1/2}$. When the heterogeneous response function is nonparametric, the panel VAR incurs a nonparametric rate loss, whereas the panel LP retains its parametric $T^{-1/2}$ rate under suitable smoothness and panel-growth conditions. We provide a Hausman-type test for choosing between them, with power against two forms of panel VAR misspecification. We apply panel LPs and panel VARs to Turkish administrative firm-level data to estimate heterogeneous firm responses to monetary policy shocks.

title: Dynamic investment in disaster preparedness under recurrent and catastrophic risks
abstract: Long-term disaster risk reduction (DRR) requires investment decisions that account for uncertain disaster conditions and accumulated preparedness capacity. This study develops a novel stochastic dynamic control model for optimal DRR investment under recurrent and catastrophic uncertainty. The model combines diffusion and Poisson jump processes and treats preparedness capital as an endogenous stock that accumulates through investment, depreciates, and mitigates economic damage. We derive a state-dependent investment rule from the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation to minimize expected discounted investment expenditure and disaster damage over an infinite horizon. Monte Carlo policy comparisons and numerical experiments examine how disaster risk structures interact with investment decisions to shape preparedness accumulation and economic losses. The results show that the economic value of DRR investment depends on adjustment to evolving conditions and disaster loss mechanisms. Lower expenditure can coexist with greater preparedness, while similar expected losses can conceal different upper-tail risks. Effective investment therefore requires attention to both accumulated preparedness and the structure of disaster risk. These findings support long-term DRR planning that integrates investment timing, capital maintenance, and recovery conditions with residual loss assessment. Upper-tail indicators complement expected-loss evaluation without being directly optimized. The framework provides a basis for dynamically managing preparedness capital.

title: Designing Behavioral Profiles for Language Model Simulation of Out-of-Distribution Human Behavior
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior, but which descriptions of people improve prediction when experimental designs change remains unclear. We develop a framework that draws candidate behavioral features from the literature and constructs profiles from earlier human experiments. An LLM-based profile generator assigns feature values from observed actions, messages, and surveys; a separate LLM simulates behavior using these profiles. By comparing simulated and observed outcomes in the training data, we select profile contents through forward feature selection, adding features while they improve prediction. We then evaluate the selected contents without modification against outcomes from new participants under new designs. Across 616 public-goods games, 144 multi-party bargaining games, and 1,480 generalized 11--20 money-request designs, leading one-feature profiles predict human outcome distributions better than no profile or general-purpose personas. Profiles with more features provide no clear additional benefit, and features' relative predictive value largely persists across learning and validation. Using profiles from one game family to simulate another produces uneven gains and can make predictions less accurate than simulations without profiles. The framework makes the choice of behavioral information a testable part of simulation design, helping researchers assess which descriptions remain useful as experimental conditions change.

title: Accessibility to Higher Education and Inter-regional Mobility
abstract: We develop an equilibrium model of the undergraduate higher education market that incorporates interregional mobility for enrollment. An individual chooses a college to attend, seeking to maximize utility depending on the quality of education and the costs of attendance. Costs include tuition fees, the effort required to pass the entrance exam, and moving costs from one's hometown to the region where the college is located. Each college admits students whose entrance exam scores exceed a certain threshold, which we call the college's qualifying score. In our model, the qualifying score of each college is determined endogenously as the shadow price of the constraint that the number of enrolled students must not exceed capacity. We structurally estimate the model's parameters by simulating equilibrium using Japanese data. Based on empirical results and counterfactual experiments, we evaluate the welfare costs of disparities in access to higher education due to uneven spatial distribution of colleges among regions.

title: Sharp Design-based Inference for Quantiles of Individual Treatment Effects
abstract: Understanding the distribution of individual treatment effects (ITEs) is a central problem in causal inference. In general, however, this distribution is only partially identifiable from observed data because it depends on the unidentifiable joint distribution of the two potential outcomes. In this paper, we develop design-based inference for the distribution of ITEs whose validity relies solely on the randomization of treatment assignment, treating the potential outcomes as arbitrary fixed constants. Building on recent randomization tests for ITE quantiles, we propose tests based on either a rank-based Kolmogorov--Smirnov (KS) statistic or the usual KS statistic, with the latter being more conservative in the presence of ties. We show that, under certain regularity conditions, the confidence bounds obtained by test inversion are asymptotically no worse than the sharp bounds on ITE quantiles given the marginal distributions of the potential outcomes. We further derive a closed-form expression for the confidence bounds from the KS-based randomization test and show that they can be equivalently constructed by combining sharp bounds on ITE quantiles with uncertainty of empirical marginal distributions. This equivalence connects randomization-based inference with partial identification and clarifies the special role of the KS statistic in achieving sharp inference. Under additional distributional assumptions, we characterize the power of the proposed randomization tests under local alternatives. Finally, we discuss how to incorporate covariates to further sharpen inference. We illustrate the properties of the proposed methods using both simulations and a real-data application.

title: Information Design for Behaviorally Stable Platooning
abstract: Voluntary platoon formation requires vehicles to coordinate despite uncertain downstream fuel savings and private joining incentives. We study whether an informed operator can encourage participation by designing a public disclosure rule. A finite-vehicle coordination game links physical fuel savings to vehicles' joining decisions under two information environments: private joining costs and private observations of the common corridor state. Private costs yield a posterior-mean participation response, while private observations require richer posterior information and create correlated formation outcomes. We formulate persuasive disclosure problems and develop computational methods for both regimes. In a literature-anchored reference scenario, optimized two-message disclosure supports participation of 8.74% and 51.83%, respectively, compared with zero without disclosure and 5.15% and 39.27% under full disclosure. Gains concentrate in intermediate opportunities, depend on joining-cost calibration, and need not maximize welfare. Numerical sensitivity and trajectory checks quantify these effects. All gains are conditional on favorable symmetric equilibrium selection: public information alone cannot eliminate the no-participation equilibrium when joining requires a costly commitment without a guaranteed partner.

title: Movement based social interactions with label uncertainty
abstract: Drone-based imagery provides high resolution data for tracking wildlife populations. However, monitoring marine mammals like cetaceans is challenging because individuals frequently submerge into water or move out of the drone's field of view, resulting in disconnected trajectories due to uncertain identities. Existing social movement models assume individual identities are known, which is often only true when data come from physical tracking devices like GPS collars. To address this limitation, we propose a Bayesian hierarchical state-space model that treats the identities associated with observed locations as unknown random variables. This allows us to jointly estimate individual movement parameters while propagating the uncertainty about identity. We apply our framework to drone-measured movement data from Risso's dolphins (Grampus griseus) to estimate the effects of sonar exposure on the dolphins' movement behavior. Our proposed method offers a solution for analyzing collective animal behavior when continuous tracking of every individual is challenging.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Pharmaceutical Development: Building Rigorous, Decision-Ready Evidence
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are reshaping the pharmaceutical lifecycle, from discovery and clinical development through manufacturing and regulatory review to safety surveillance and health economics, creating evidentiary challenges that predictive performance alone cannot address. This review examines the inferential, causal, validation, and documentation requirements for AI-enabled evidence generation in high-stakes settings and argues that they must be built into workflows. We outline the evidentiary functions that AI-derived outputs must satisfy before supporting consequential decisions: estimand definition, fit-for-purpose data collection, bias control, uncertainty quantification, validation, interpretability, and decision-grade documentation. Because AI both depends on and accelerates large-scale, non-randomized data collection, the integration of randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with real-world data (RWD) is where its evidentiary risks concentrate; we therefore present a five-step causal roadmap for that integration, in which external data supplement but never replace a concurrent control, and characterize the safeguards required across development, pharmacovigilance, regulation, and health technology assessment. Priority frontiers answer recurring implementation problems: conformal prediction for overconfident predictions, randomization-based inference for scarce data, and federated causal inference and privacy-preserving generative modeling for data that cannot be pooled. Evidence generation depends not on competition between RCTs and RWD, or between statistics and AI/ML, but on their principled synthesis under causal and inferential frameworks, with statistical expertise central to decision-ready evidence.

title: Efficient Causal Survival Inference under Limited Surrogate Monitoring
abstract: Post-treatment surrogate endpoints can improve the efficiency of causal survival effect estimation, but their monitoring may end before follow-up for the primary outcome. We investigate the impact of limited recurrence monitoring on semiparametric efficiency when mortality follow-up continues. We derive the efficient influence function under limited monitoring and establish an exact expression for the efficiency gain from extending monitoring between any two durations. Our framework encompasses the absence of surrogate information and the usual shared-censoring scheme as boundary cases, and allows comparison with fully observed surrogates. We develop a doubly robust estimator under limited surrogate monitoring and establish asymptotic normality and semiparametric efficiency for its cross-fitted version under suitable conditions. Simulations and an application to breast cancer data illustrate the proposed method.

title: Characterizing Estimator-Regime Transitions in Adaptive Enrichment Trials
abstract: Adaptive enrichment trials that identify responsive subpopulations allocate a fixed sample across them and estimate each one's effect from the resulting data. For a synthetic control design with adaptive recruitment and borrowing of control outcomes, we ask whether a doubly robust family of targeted maximum likelihood estimators should replace its sample mean; the choice can be made largely at the design stage. A crossing condition weighs the bias removed and the efficiency gained by the doubly robust family against the finite-sample inflation of nuisance estimation; an equal-error boundary, located by simulation, separates the families in the plane of sample size and bias. A consistency principle prices recruiting with the wrong family's variance functional. With three and eight simulated subpopulations the boundary's sign prediction for the mean squared error difference holds in $99.6\%$ of $10{,}302$ comparisons decided at two standard errors. A pre-specified selector commits to the doubly robust family where the squared anticipated bias exceeds the net variance term. Recruiting along that family's path costs up to $0.035$ in the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve; recruiting with the sample mean functional and routing only the analysis removes this cost and about nine tenths of its error excess.

title: FIXP-Completeness in Second-Price Auctions
abstract: Computing equilibria is a fundamental algorithmic problem in game theory and economics. Although general frameworks are available for proving membership in FIXP, the class capturing exact fixed-point computation, establishing FIXP-completeness often remains challenging. We prove FIXP-completeness of exact equilibrium computation in three second-price auction models: (1). pacing with return-on-investment constraints, with multiplier cap $1+\delta$ for every fixed rational $\delta>0$ [Filos-Ratsikas, Hansen, H{\o}gh, and Hollender (2024)]; (2). budget-constrained generalized second-price sponsored shopping [Hansen, Li, and Nie (2026)]; (3). budget-constrained throttling [Liu (2026)]. These results resolve open questions on the exact complexity of automated bidding. Our technical ingredient is a FIXP-complete generalized-circuit problem using only clipped affine gates and the reciprocal $x\mapsto1/(1+\tau x)$, for any fixed positive rational $\tau$. This gate basis provides a common framework for the three auction reductions: simulating these gates in each model establishes FIXP-hardness without directly implementing multiplication or squaring.

title: Multiplicity and Uniqueness of Stationary Expected Payoffs in Coalitional Bargaining
abstract: I study uniqueness of stationary expected payoffs in random-proposer coalitional bargaining with transferable utility. Proposer independence of coalition surplus does not guarantee uniqueness, even when the surplus is strictly monotone and every equilibrium features immediate agreement. For $M^\natural$-concave characteristic functions, including non-monotone ones, I show that stationary expected payoffs are unique and continuous in the primitives, provided that every equilibrium features immediate agreement. To prove uniqueness, I identify an equitable grouping property of maximizing coalitions and show that $M^\natural$-concavity implies it at every no-delay candidate payoff vector. Using equitable grouping, I show that every no-delay equilibrium payoff vector is isolated and has positive local index. For parameter changes that preserve immediate agreement in every equilibrium, a uniform increase in a player's contribution to every coalition containing her strictly increases her expected payoff, while an increase in her discount factor weakly increases it. I apply these results to joint ventures with coordination costs and government formation with ministerial expertise.

title: Robust Inference for Spiked Eigenspace under Elliptical Distributions
abstract: In this paper, we study two eigenspace testing problems under high-dimensional elliptical spiked models: whether the spiked eigenspace equals a given subspace, and whether a given vector is a spike eigenvector. We propose a \textbf{Robust Functional Projection} (RFP) test and a \textbf{Robust Spike Direction} (RSD) test for these two problems, respectively. Based on the spatial-sign covariance matrix $\bm C_n$, both tests achieve robustness by remaining invariant to the radial distribution without moment conditions and allowing the background level to be unknown. To construct and analyze both tests, we establish central limit theorems for \textbf{G}eneralized \textbf{E}lliptical \textbf{S}patial-sign \textbf{S}pectral statistics (GESS) $\operatorname{tr}\{f(\bm C_n)\bm B_n\}$. The results cover a general class of deterministic weighting matrices $\bm B_n$ whose ranks are either comparable to the dimension or of smaller order, providing a common theoretical foundation for both tests. The central idea in constructing both tests is to avoid the need for consistent estimations of individual spike eigenvalues by working directly with GESS. Simulations illustrate the finite-sample performance of the procedures, and an analysis of LOCATA acoustic data demonstrates their use in assessing a signal subspace and a steering direction, both constructed from measured source and array geometry.

title: Time-Specific Multinomial Logistic Regression for Competing Risks
abstract: Motivated by the project on premature menopause among childhood cancer survivors in the Childhood Cancer Survivor Study (CCSS), we develop methods for estimating time-specific factor effects using doubly censored event time data with competing risks. We begin with fitting separate binary logistic regression models for different causes. However, the approach does not ensure the sum of the resulting estimated cumulative incidence rates remains bounded by one. To overcome this limitation, we consider a multinomial logistic regression formulation to jointly model all cause-specific risks. Two inverse-probability-of-censoring-weight (IPCW) based estimating functions are proposed accordingly. To handle the estimation instability caused by data separation, we incorporate the Firth-type penalization in those estimating functions to obtain more stable coefficient estimators. The sandwich variance estimator is applied to estimate the standard errors. A weighted quasi-likelihood information criterion, paired with a backward elimination, is further adapted to the proposed estimating functions for selecting covariates at a given age. Simulation studies are conducted to examine the proposed approaches regarding consistency, efficiency, and robustness of the estimators. The Firth correction substantially reduces the bias induced by separation and provides valid standard error estimation. We illustrate the proposed approach with the CCSS data viewing premature ovarian insufficiency and surgical premature menopause as the two potential causes of the primary event, premature menopause. The data analysis reveals that the effects of the cancer treatment-related covariates are significant on premature ovarian insufficiency but not on surgical premature menopause. The variable selection procedure, illustrated on an extended covariate set, yields estimated risks close to those under the full model.

title: Power-Optimal Risk Control via Standardized Margin Calibration
abstract: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.

title: Penalized Likelihood Inference in Highly Multivariate Sparse Spectral Graphical Gaussian Processes
abstract: We develop a penalized likelihood inference approach for highly multivariate Gaussian stochastic processes. Since zeros in the inverse cross-spectral density encode process-level conditional independence, sparse modeling of this object provides a natural route to scalable inference in the highly multivariate case. We introduce a latent variable representation which, combined with random Fourier features, yields a stochastic approximation expectation--maximization algorithm for penalized maximum likelihood estimation of a sparse inverse cross-spectral density matrix under a graphical LASSO penalty. The augmentation is crucial because sparsity is present in the inverse spectral density of the latent variable, whereas the marginal inverse covariance remains dense in the presence of a spatial nugget. Our frequency domain formulation enables joint penalized likelihood estimation of process-specific spatial covariance parameters and sparse process-level conditional dependence without requiring a pre-specified reference set of locations. The method is demonstrated on both synthetic and the MERRA-2 aerosol reanalysis data sets, yielding benefit over existing alternatives, especially for prediction at unobserved locations under spatial misalignment.

title: Siting and Curtailment Depth Limit the Grid Headroom Available to New Large Loads
abstract: Data center demand is increasing faster than generation can be built, encouraging proposals to interconnect large loads on condition that they reduce consumption during high-stress periods. Estimates of how much load can be added via flexibility rest on simplified accounting and report only annual curtailed electricity. Here we use a national energy systems model that co-optimizes hourly generation and load curtailment across 16 U.S. regions to characterize the flexibility and power system impacts of enabling headroom. While 50 GW can be served while curtailing less than 0.1% of its annual energy, small annual curtailment conceals potentially severe operating requirements. Most regions require curtailment deeper than 90% in at least one hour, so the load must disconnect or have sufficient on-site resources to provide full back up. Furthermore, announced data center locations are not aligned with modeled headroom and relying on existing generation fleets raises CO2 emissions and wholesale electricity prices.

title: Online Fair Division of Chores with Upgrade Recourse
abstract: We study the online fair division of indivisible chores among $n$ agents under upgrade recourse, where earlier assignments may be revised but each chore previously assigned to an agent must be replaced by a distinct chore that she finds no more costly. We show that a simple adaptation of round robin maintains envy-freeness up to one chore (EF1) together with a $(2-1/n)$-approximation of the maximin share (MMS), and that no deterministic algorithm without predictions can do better, even when all agents rank the chores in the same order. This stands in contrast to the allocation of goods, where the optimal MMS factor vanishes as $n$ grows and cannot be achieved together with EF1. Moreover, knowing only the number of chores modulo a period of length $O(n)$ (and nothing about the costs) suffices to improve upon this factor at the final configuration, while the same algorithm retains a factor below $3$ even if this information is wrong. On the other hand, envy-freeness up to any chore (EFX) essentially requires the exact number of chores: uncertainty between two consecutive values already rules out every finite approximation, and even exact knowledge does not allow EFX to be combined with an MMS guarantee better than the trivial factor of $n$.

title: Vector incremental treatment effects
abstract: Causal questions involving multiple binary treatments are poorly served by standard causal approaches. Potential outcomes grow exponentially with the number of treatments, many treatment combinations are rarely or never observed, and fixing everyone to one combination can require implausible positivity assumptions. We extend incremental propensity score interventions to vector-valued binary treatments, defining causal effects through counterfactual distributions that scale the odds of each treatment by a user-specified factor. Because marginal odds constraints do not uniquely determine the joint distribution, we define it as the minimum-divergence projection of the observed law onto the constrained set, for a user-specified separable divergence, preserving the observed conditional support. The resulting counterfactual mean outcome is identified under consistency and conditional mean exchangeability, without requiring every treatment combination to have positive conditional probability. For a class of smooth divergences, we derive the efficient influence function and construct cross-fitted one-step estimators that are consistent at the parametric rate and asymptotically normal when marginal treatment probabilities are exactly 0, exactly 1, or bounded away from those values. We relax this requirement by specifying a different estimand and deriving a corresponding estimator, which is asymptotically normal under a convergence-rate condition on the estimated active set. We also extend sensitivity analysis to address unmeasured confounding. Applying the framework to 159,466 New York Medicaid beneficiaries with serious mental illness, we estimate how healthcare costs would change under uniform improvements in the odds of six recommended quality-of-care processes. Increasing recommended care is associated with lower total, inpatient, and mental-health cost and higher outpatient cost.

title: Transformer-Based Reinforcement Learning for Phase I Dose Allocation
abstract: Phase I dose-finding trials must learn from sparse toxicity observations while limiting exposure to overly toxic doses. We develop a single reinforcement-learning policy for trials with different numbers of ordered dose levels. Each dose is represented as a token containing its normalized position, accumulated patient count, observed dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs), and current-dose indicator. A Transformer encoder summarizes the dose tokens, trial-conditioned cross-attention produces a fixed-dimensional trial representation, and a three-action policy chooses de-escalation, staying, or escalation. The final maximum tolerated dose (MTD) decision is deliberately kept outside the learned policy: after the planned sample size, weighted isotonic regression and a prespecified safety cap select the dose closest to the target toxicity probability. In the simulations, toxicity-penalized policies reduce DLT burden while unpenalized policies improve selection accuracy at the cost of greater toxicity. These results demonstrate a controllable safety--accuracy trade-off but do not establish superiority over conventional dose-finding designs.

title: Statistical Sheaf Modeling Methods for Measuring Qualia Structures
authors: Donna A. Dietz and Michael Robinson
abstract: Mathematical sheaves are an abstraction that captures the notion that consistency between local properties can lead to a global picture. There are a number of (mathematical) phenomena that sheaves exhibit, which seem tantalizingly close to what one might hope a theory of qualia would explain. Recently, the theory and abstraction of sheaves has been transformed into robust computational tools for understanding complex systems. These tools are now ripe to help qualia researchers forge robust and testable models. Intuitively, as conscious entities, rather than experiencing ``everything all at once,'' our experience is coherent to varying degrees. Sheaves can model this rather nicely. This chapter presents the practical and theoretical considerations of sheaves in data modeling, with a view towards computational models that can support statistical hypothesis testing.

title: Robustness of Median-based Splitting Rules for Causal Trees
abstract: Causal forests (Athey and Imbens, 2016) are a widely used method for the estimation of heterogeneous treatment effects. Standard implementations use mean-based splitting criteria, which perform well when the outcome distribution is well-behaved and free of contamination, such as outliers or heavy tails. However, real-world data are rarely clean. Outcome perturbations can affect the tree structure selected by mean-based splitting rules and lead to unreliable treatment effect estimates. In this study, we systematically examine the robustness of causal forests to irregularities in the outcome distribution. Building on the median-based splitting criteria introduced by Ma{\ss}mann and Gliszczy\'nska-Schroeder (2026), we empirically investigate three median-based splitting criteria: Median Absolute Deviation (MAD), Least Median of Squares (LMS), and Median Squared Deviation (MSD). We conduct Monte Carlo experiments and apply the methods to empirical benchmark datasets from the causal inference literature to compare the performance of the median-based approaches with standard causal forests. We additionally examine pointwise confidence interval coverage using the Bootstrap of Little Bags and the infinitesimal jackknife. The results indicate that median-based splitting criteria can reduce sensitivity to outcome irregularities in specific scenarios, particularly in the presence of extreme heavy-tailed noise and nonlinear treatment effect heterogeneity. However, these benefits are scenario-dependent and do not consistently lead to more accurate conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.

title: Reading the Count: Prediction Markets and Brazil's 2026 Presidential Election
abstract: We rebuild the public count of Brazil's 2026 presidential runoff minute by minute from the electoral court's section-level records and compare it with every trade on Kalshi and Polymarket. A projection published live on the night gave the eventual winner, Lula, a probability of 0.998 from 19:15, with 1.6% of sections counted. The markets reached 0.9 at 20:24, with 46% counted. Read as the projection's central estimate with a wider uncertainty, their prices imply a standard deviation of the final margin about four times the live projection's, and about twice that of a section-level projection calibrated on the 2018 runoff, the earlier night with the largest errors. Valued at these projections, takers' purchases of Lula after the count resumed had an expected profit of 4 to 18 cents per Kalshi contract after fees; valued at a state-level extrapolation of the count, it was zero. During a two-hour suspension of the count the markets gave Lula 0.25 to 0.44, below every reading we compute afterwards from the sections then public, none of which was available live. On the first-round night, when the headline count showed the eventual leader ahead from its first file, the same markets were faster than our projection.

title: Robust Estimation of Prior Parameters in Normal-Normal Empirical Bayes
abstract: Many large-scale A/B testing systems leverage normal-normal empirical Bayes models to improve estimates of treatment impacts and launch decisions. We show that in these models maximum likelihood estimates of the variance of true impacts can be sensitive to a small number of extreme observations. We propose a bounded influence maximum likelihood estimator (BIMLE) that downweights such observations in proportion to their inconsistency with the model, reducing sensitivity while retaining the full sample in estimation. Absent extreme observations, BIMLE coincides with the standard MLE. In an application to A/B tests run at Amazon, BIMLE reduces instability in the estimated prior variance by over 50 percent while downweighting less than 0.1 percent of observations.

title: Decomposition Atlases of Brains and Kidneys from Postmortem CT: Shape and Topological Data Analysis
abstract: Forensic assessments of postmortem decomposition often rely on external, whole-body signs, yet structural changes within organs remain largely unquantified. Using whole-body computed tomography scans of 59 decedents from the New Mexico Decedent Image Database, we conduct an organ-level statistical shape analysis of decomposing brains and kidneys, representing each organ as a three-dimensional point cloud of its outer surface and internal cavity boundaries. Decomposition creates voids, fragmentation, and structural heterogeneity, complicating point correspondence. Registration-based principal component analysis and principal nested cones yield interpretable orderings for brains only. We therefore construct a registration-free pipeline using persistent homology and a fusion of complementary topological distances selected through simulations of cavity formation and growth. Clustering identifies broad patterns of internal decay, and seriation produces organ-specific decomposition atlases. The brain atlas combines geometric and topological rankings; the kidney atlas uses topology alone. Rank agreement is higher between paired kidneys (Kendall's $\tau = 0.59$) than between brains and kidneys ($\tau = 0.34$ to $0.39$), indicating asynchronous decompositions within a body. Whole-body stages agree more closely with brain than with kidney rankings. These findings support quantitative forensic taphonomy by complementing whole-body staging with organ-level, interior-based measurements. We release the organ point clouds and analysis code to support research on organ decomposition and shape analysis without reliable correspondence.

title: Outstrumental Variable Regression
abstract: Estimating the causal effect of a treatment $X$ on an outcome $Y$ from observational data in the presence of unobserved confounding requires additional structure or assumptions. Existing identification strategies such as instrumental variable regression exploit exogenous variation in only the treatment. We show that the causal effect can also be identified if the outcome mechanism varies across a finite set of environments, even if the treatment distribution is unchanged. Concretely, we introduce Outstrumental Variable Regression (OVR), which proceeds in three steps: (i) compute the conditional expectation of $Y$ given $X$ in each environment; (ii) form the vector of differences in these conditional expectations between all environments and a reference environment (we call this vector contrast); and (iii) regress $Y$ on $X$ while adjusting for the contrast and environment. We prove that this yields the true causal effect if the following two conditions hold: inclusion restriction, i.e., the contrast determines the conditional confounding bias; and positivity, i.e., the treatment varies sufficiently strongly after adjustment. We prove that a finite-sample version of OVR is consistent under regularity conditions and demonstrate the procedure's effectiveness on synthetic and real-world data.

title: Validating LLM-Generated Synthetic Survey Samples: A Use-Dependent Multi-Dimensional Framework for Social-Science Applications
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) make it increasingly feasible to generate synthetic survey respondents, but their empirical usefulness cannot be judged by a single notion of accuracy. A synthetic sample may perform weakly at the respondent level while still preserving distributional or substantive relationships relevant to social-science analysis. We develop a use-dependent, multi-dimensional validation framework distinguishing predictive, distributional, and substantive validity, and illustrate it using Eurobarometer data on attitudes toward artificial intelligence. Four off-the-shelf LLMs generate responses conditional on observed respondent profiles, while supervised machine learning provides a predictive reference for interpreting their performance. The results reveal substantial differences across validation dimensions: some LLM-generated samples preserve meaningful marginal heterogeneity, demographic ordering, cross-country variation, and predictor structure despite imperfect respondent-level correspondence. Performance varies across models and outcomes, but the broader picture is cautiously constructive. Synthetic samples should therefore be evaluated against the empirical properties required by their intended use.

title: Value of Adding AI Weather Model Ensembles to a Multi-model Probabilistic Blend
abstract: Many weather forecasting organizations use a multi-model blend of ensemble members from different prediction systems to obtain a more accurate forecast. Recent studies have shown that blending deterministic AI-based models alongside physics-based models improves the overall forecast skill. However, the incorporation of an ensemble AI-based model into a multi-model blend is yet to be investigated. This study explores the value of blending the ensemble version of the Artificial Intelligence Forecasting System (AIFS-CRPS) with the Met Office's convection permitting physics-based ensemble, MOGREPS-UK. We show that blending site temperature (and wind speed) forecasts over the United Kingdom from both ensemble physics-based and ensemble AI-based models leads to an increase in overall forecast skill spatially, across lead times and across exceedance thresholds, especially when the models have different error characteristics. By decomposing the continuous ranked probability score of the blend into component means and diversity terms, we show that a more accurate blend can be achieved by assigning more weight to more skillful models and using models with complementary errors. For example, we show that a blend of MOGREPS-UK with either AIFS-CRPS or the physics-based Integrated Forecasting System (IFS) is better than a blend of IFS and AIFS-CRPS which are not very diverse. This has implications for the importance of weather model diversity and may lend weight to different model development approaches being pursued in tandem. We also demonstrate that calibrating AIFS-CRPS forecasts yields an increase in forecast skill comparable to calibrated ensemble physics-based forecasts, and calibrating the source forecasts before blending and the blended forecast after blending improves the overall forecast accuracy.

title: Co-sufficient weighting: leveraging sparsity for more powerful variable selection in the linear model
abstract: We show that for the problem of controlled variable selection in the Gaussian linear model, informative and p-value-independent weights (for weighted multiple testing) can be derived entirely from sufficient statistics and a belief in sparsity using only the data itself and no external quantitative side information. Using these weights, which we call \emph{co-sufficient weights} (CSW), in weighted versions of Holm's procedure and the Benjamini--Hochberg (BH) procedure results in substantially higher power than their unweighted analogues when the true coefficient vector is sparse, while retaining Holm's exact validity and BH's highly robust empirical validity regardless of sparsity. We demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed weighted methods compared to their unweighted analogues and other competing methods in a wide range of simulations and an application to HIV drug resistance.

title: Strategic Tanking in Stable Matching Markets
abstract: Motivated by a broad literature in psychology, organizational behavior, and matching markets, we introduce strategic tanking: an agent deliberately makes themselves less attractive to selected potential partners in order to improve their eventual assignment. Unlike traditional manipulation in stable matching, a tanker does not misreport whom they prefer; instead, they influence how others rank them. We show that tanking has a striking connection to classical preference manipulation. Cutoff tanking, in which an agent tanks with every potential partner below a chosen threshold, has exactly the same effect on the stable set as truncating one's own preference list at that threshold. Thus an agent can reproduce the power of a classical truncation while leaving their own preferences unchanged and every match acceptable. Arbitrary tanking, however, can go substantially further: under proposer-deferred acceptance, tanking equilibria can lie outside the sincere stable set. More broadly, whenever the sincere stable set contains multiple matchings, profitable strategic behavior remains available through either traditional preference manipulation or tanking, even when one side is restricted to honestly reporting their own preferences.

title: From Scalar Games to Unconstrained Network Zero-Sum Games: Transfer Principles for Gradient-Based Learning
abstract: We show that, for a broad class of gradient-based learning rules, scalar zero-sum games form a complete test family for convergence in unconstrained network zero-sum games. Specifically, suppose a learning rule achieves last-iterate or time-average convergence on every scalar game of magnitude $a$ whenever $\eta\leq f(a)$, where $f$ is nonincreasing. Then the same guarantee holds on an arbitrary network zero-sum game with stacked game operator $\mathbf{G}$ whenever $\eta\leq f(\lVert\mathbf{G}\rVert_2)$. More generally, finite-time rate guarantees transfer mode by mode: the network response is bounded by the largest response of its scalar canonical games, and under compatible linear initialization conventions the worst-case finite-time network response is exactly the largest scalar canonical rate. Thus, understanding the learning dynamics on scalar games is sufficient to characterize universal convergence and worst-case rates over the corresponding class of network games. The result follows from the classical planar decomposition of real skew-symmetric game operators. Related mode-wise reasoning has appeared implicitly in spectral analyses of particular learning algorithms and in prior work using these decompositions for game representation and visualization; here we isolate the resulting transfer principle for gradient-based learning. We discuss implications for simplifying convergence analysis, time-average guarantees, low-dimensional geometric arguments, accelerated-method design, and worst-case numerical testing.

title: Valid GMM Inference with Non-parametrically Generated Discrete Type
abstract: The recent progress in machine learning and classification methods has enabled researchers to predict economic discrete attributes that are not observed in standard datasets. These range from missing demographics, such as ethnicity and poverty status, to economic categories, such as innovative firms, metropolitan areas, occupational groups, binary treatment status, and counterfactual status. Although the plug-in procedure is widely used in empirical applications, nonparametric first-stage estimation recovering the labels can introduce regularization bias because of its slow convergence rate. Even if the double/debiased machine learning approach provides a way to correct the regularization bias, the according bias-correction term is not well defined in our problem, because even a small first-stage error can change the type discontinuously. To address this problem, we smooth the discontinuous type indicators using a smooth kernel function and a shrinking tuning parameter $b$. We then construct a well-defined Neyman-orthogonal score and define the appropriate debiased estimator. We show that this debiased estimator satisfies $\sqrt{Nb}$-consistency and asymptotic normality under regularity conditions. The slower $\sqrt{Nb}$ convergence rate is the cost of correcting the regularization bias when the nonparametric first-stage learner enters the moment function through discontinuous functions.

title: Zero Crossings on the Accuracy-Smoothness Frontier: Maximal Monotone and Minimal Inflection Non Stationary Predictors
abstract: The Smooth Sign Accuracy (SSA) framework resolves the smoothness--accuracy dilemma for stationary predictors by balancing mean squared error (MSE) against the frequency of sign changes. We generalize it to non-stationary integrated processes (I-SSA), deriving MSE-optimal predictors constrained by the expected duration between turning points (I(1)) or inflection points (I(2)). The resulting maximal-monotone and minimal-inflection predictors, filters, and smoothers customize classic benchmarks along a new efficient Accuracy--Smoothness (AS) frontier. Tracking the identity (the original data) along this frontier defines the \emph{I-SSA trend}, a novel smoothing concept that, unlike classical filters, imposes no artificial structure on the data-generating process and is directly interpretable through explicit control of turning- or inflection-point frequency. The optimization is a quadratically constrained quadratic program (QCQP) that reduces to a Generalized Trust Region Subproblem (GTRS) with hidden convexity. On its feasible, invertible region the problem is convex with a well-defined global optimum, and an exact closed-form expression delivers the efficient AS frontier. Under fairly general assumptions, finite-sample solutions converge to an asymptotic I-SSA predictor, devoid of integration boundary perturbations. The framework unifies mean squared error on non-stationary levels, and sign accuracy, zero-crossing frequency, and target correlation on stationary differences.

title: When Is a Game a Markov Decision Process? Correspondences Between Game Theory and Reinforcement Learning
abstract: Reinforcement learning and game theory describe the same object from two sides. Game theory says what a rational outcome of a strategic interaction is; reinforcement learning says how an agent could reach one through experience. The two literatures nevertheless keep separate vocabularies for identical structures, and the treatments that bridge them present the correspondence as analogy rather than theorem. This monograph supplies the theorems. A game is a Markov decision process in three distinct senses, and every table entry is labelled with the one that applies: a definitional identity, an exact reduction carried by a value- and solution-preserving map, or a structural analogy that fails under identifiable conditions. We take every standard class of game, from normal-form through repeated, stochastic, partially observable, extensive-form with imperfect information, Bayesian, graphical, Stackelberg, potential, coalitional, mean-field and evolutionary games, and identify for each the decision-theoretic model that reinforcement learning already studies under another name. The same treatment is applied to solution concepts: Nash equilibrium and the fixed point of the Bellman optimality operator, quantal response equilibrium and the soft Bellman operator, the Shapley value and credit assignment, Blackwell approachability and no-regret learning. We map each model class onto the training procedures sound for it and record the complexity of the associated solution problems. A final part collects the correspondences that do not hold: the non-stationarity that invalidates the independent-learner reduction, the impossibility results that forbid uncoupled convergence to Nash equilibrium, and the gap between the coarse correlated equilibria that no-regret self-play reaches and the correlated equilibria it is credited with.

title: A Semiparametric Model Approach to Data Integration under Missing Not at Random
abstract: Integrating probability and non-probability samples requires accounting for an unknown selection mechanism that may depend on the outcome. We develop a semiparametric approach in which an unspecified function captures covariate dependence and a scalar tilting parameter governs outcome dependence. Identification follows from an instrumental-variable exclusion restriction and conditional completeness; a zero tilt gives a restricted missing-at-random submodel. We profile out the covariate component and construct cross-fitted, Neyman-orthogonal estimating equations for both the tilting parameter and the finite population mean. The resulting orthogonalized mass-imputation estimator supports centered root-N inference under nuisance product-rate conditions. Its linearization variance accounts for the probability sampling design and estimation of the tilting parameter. Simulations illustrate the cost of flexibility under correct parametric specification, protection against misspecification of the covariate component, and the consequences of invalid instruments or a misspecified tilt. A further simulation using 50,000 national health-screening records finds smaller bias but higher root mean squared error than a parametric competitor under the baseline instrument set. The proposed estimator varies less across alternative instrument sets, although weak instruments and smoothing choices affect precision and interval coverage.

title: Parametric inference for the average hazard approach in time-to-event analysis with sparse risk sets
abstract: The average hazard (AH) is a recently proposed model-free summary of an event-time distribution. Over a prespecified window $[0,\tau]$, it equals the cumulative incidence probability at $\tau$ divided by the restricted mean survival time at $\tau$ and can be interpreted as a person-time incidence rate that does not depend on the censoring distribution. The difference and ratio of AHs from two groups, DAH and RAH, are between-group contrasts on absolute and relative scales without requiring proportional hazards. Existing nonparametric inference for AH and its contrasts is based on the Kaplan--Meier estimator of the survival function, and can become unreliable when risk sets become sparse or exhausted near $\tau$, as may occur in stratified analyses. As a practical remedy, we investigate parametric AH inference using Weibull and generalized gamma models. We use maximum-likelihood estimators and corresponding confidence intervals for group-specific AHs, DAH and RAH in both unstratified and stratified analyses. Simulations show that under correct model specification, little bias and near-nominal coverage can be achieved in settings where nonparametric inference is inadequately supported by observed data. We illustrate the method using a randomized trial comparing neratinib plus capecitabine with lapatinib plus capecitabine in metastatic breast cancer. Parametric inference provides a practical complement to nonparametric AH analysis when sparse or exhausted risk sets make inference at clinically relevant truncation times less reliable.

title: Unifying Data-Adaptive Longitudinal Treatment-Effect Subgroup Discovery and Pretreatment Membership Prediction
abstract: Precision medicine seeks to match patients with treatments from which they are most likely to benefit. A key step toward this goal is to learn treatment-effect heterogeneity from longitudinal study data. This requires discovering subgroups with distinct treatment-effect trajectories and predicting subgroup membership for new patients from pretreatment information. Existing methods do not fully unify these tasks. Covariate-informed membership models typically prespecify the subgroup number or covariance structure, whereas data-adaptive discovery methods often require prediction in a separate stage. We propose a data-adaptive semiparametric mixture-of-experts framework that unifies longitudinal treatment-effect subgroup discovery and pretreatment membership prediction. Subgroup-specific varying-coefficient functions characterize treatment-effect trajectories, while flexible covariance functions account for within-subject dependence. A covariate-dependent gating model links membership to pretreatment characteristics. A penalty on global component weights removes redundant subgroups, while separate gating coefficients allow patient-specific membership probabilities among retained subgroups. A blockwise generalized expectation--maximization algorithm estimates all model components under a single penalized observed-data objective. We establish consistent subgroup-number selection, convergence rates for the functional estimators, and asymptotic normality for the finite-dimensional parameters. Simulations show reliable subgroup-number selection and more accurate conditional membership prediction than a two-step procedure. Applications to the SANAD epilepsy study and the COMPETE migraine trial identify distinct temporal treatment-effect patterns.

title: Evaluating Maternity Leave Reforms When RD Fails
authors: Clara von Bismarck-Osten and Andrei Zeleneev
abstract: This paper documents that expansions of UK maternity pay in the 2000s improved children's test scores while reducing maternal employment. Extending job protection alone generated similar employment effects but no detectable impact on children. None of these effects are recoverable with a conventional regression discontinuity (RD) design because eligibility is only imperfectly captured by the available data. We explain why existing corrections for measurement error in RD are not well suited and propose a simple imputation-based solution. The approach preserves RD's main advantages, nonparametric identification and transparency, and remains valid even when measurement error has economic content.

title: Observation-Specific Uncertainty Modeling for Latent-Variable Regression in High-Dimensional Analytical Data
abstract: Across many fields, including medical diagnostics, process monitoring, and quality control, decisions often rely on point predictions for single samples. Observation-specific uncertainty is needed to assess the risk of decision error when predictions are compared with thresholds. Latent-variable regression is widely used for such predictions, but observation-specific uncertainty remains difficult to estimate. Traditional methods assume unbiased predictions, attributing prediction uncertainty solely to variance. However, dimensionality reduction can introduce observation-specific bias, violating this assumption. We introduce a framework using Gaussian processes trained on latent scores and prediction errors to estimate observation-specific bias and error variance, separating systematic error from epistemic and aleatoric variance. In Raman measurements of a fructose-sucrose model system, estimated prediction-error distributions agreed with empirical distributions; bias correction reduced mean squared error, and decision limits incorporating bias and variance improved analyte detection over variance-only limits. An aqueous-solubility application using molecular descriptors demonstrated the framework's generalisation beyond spectroscopy.

title: Functional-Specific Information Borrowing under Limited Overlap
abstract: Source observations can improve a target average without estimating the entire shared response accurately. We study this distinction in two independent observational samples whose treatment effects share a rough component and differ by a smoother discrepancy. For power-law treatment overlap known for the analysis, known design density, fixed positive Sobolev radii, and Gaussian noise, we derive matching minimax mean squared error bounds with three regimes. Two explicit source-information thresholds determine the onset of rate improvement and attainment of the source-known rate. A signed local correction explains the thresholds: source observations estimate only the part of the integration functional poorly recovered from the target sample. Direct likelihood lower bounds apply to all estimators. Existing joint reproducing-kernel recovery, which does not require propensity inputs, attains these rates, and standard bias-aware intervals are conditionally honest under the specified class. A supplementary zero-overlap result separates estimation error from residual identification uncertainty. Numerical results illustrate both gains and losses when the total number of participants is fixed. The intermediate rate depends on overlap geometry, while smoothness determines its two endpoints.

title: Unidentified prediction-risk rankings under spatial sampling with fixed inclusion probabilities
abstract: For Gaussian spatial prediction, we construct positive sampling mechanisms with identical observation laws and conditional site inclusion probabilities, yet opposite risk rankings for two fixed predictors. The construction selects two of four sites and allows independent Gaussian measurement error.

title: Covariance Identification from Regression Residuals
abstract: Regression residuals are projections of the errors, not observations of them. This paper characterizes what residuals identify about the error covariance. Residualization acts on the covariance through a known linear map, and under an unrestricted covariance model the directions it destroys are exactly those generated by the column space of the regressors. A linear covariance functional is identified if and only if it does not load on these lost directions, and restricting the covariance model, for instance to diagonal or clustered form, shrinks them. The central result separates projection loss from moment-selection loss: projecting the residual covariance onto the maintained covariance structure loses no identifying information, so cross-cluster, long-lag, and long-distance residual products add no identifying directions. They can still improve conditioning, since restricting to the aligned moments squares the condition number. This equivalence relies on the orthogonal-projection geometry of OLS, and generally fails for non-orthogonal transformation. Quadratic statistics in the outcome that are free of the regression coefficients additionally identify the covariance between the fitted and residual components, but not the covariance within the span of the regressors. Because the OLS sandwich variance depends only on that block, it is not identified by any such statistic under an unrestricted covariance model; robust variance estimation draws its identification from maintained restrictions on the covariance structure.

title: From fleet trajectories to single-cell promises: hierarchically weighted conformal prediction for battery SOH monitoring
abstract: Interval predictions from conformal prediction are usually read as "90% coverage", but on nested battery data that number promises the fleet average, not the individual cell. We measure the gap on 124 public LFP cells under a preregistered three-tier reporting protocol (fleet, batch, cell): pooled coverage looks healthy (0.875-0.906 across splits) while the worst cell is covered 0.1-2% of the time, with exact binomial tests against the nominal level. We then repair part of the gap with a hierarchically weighted conformal engine whose weights consume only side information frozen at prediction time - signature features, batch labels, cycle indices - and never touch residuals. The preregistered repair criterion passes: 10th-percentile cell coverage moves 0.750 to 0.830 (53% of the gap), the worst cell 0.642 to 0.694, with zero deferrals and a flat sensitivity spectrum. What the engine does not repair is localized rather than left open: under protocol drift the frozen weights harm monotonically on the SOH scale (the absolute scale is reported in full), a structural dead end we report instead of tuning away; and repair capacity is bounded by calibration-pool battery diversity, measured on both datasets. On a cross-chemistry external set the calibrated intervals collapse (0.286), while the within-domain skeleton replicates (pooled 0.933, worst cell 0.686). The deliverable is a reporting protocol - three tiers of promise anchored to measured regimes, worst-cell statistics, deferral share - that makes per-cell interval claims auditable before deployment.

title: Stable and efficient covariance estimation for sample L-moments using H\'ajek projections
abstract: L-moments are useful summary statistics and are widely used in statistical analysis. The joint covariance matrix of sample L-moments not only describes their sampling uncertainty but is also needed for covariance-weighted distances and related statistical procedures. An exact unbiased covariance estimator is already available. However, in our previous applications, this estimator sometimes produced singular or indefinite covariance matrices. Such matrices cause problems when matrix inversion is required. The present paper addresses this difficulty. We examine standard positive-definite corrections and two covariance estimators based on leave-one-out sample L-moments: the delete-one jackknife estimator and an estimator based on the H\'ajek projection. Both are positive semidefinite by construction. Simulation results show that the projection estimator generally has smaller estimation error and better numerical stability than the exact unbiased estimator. The jackknife estimator overestimates the variances of higher-order sample L-moments and has larger estimation error than the projection estimator. We also develop fast rank-prefix algorithms for the three covariance estimators considered. These algorithms substantially reduce computation time.

title: Uncertainty Quantification for Topological Treatment Effects
abstract: We present a unified framework for uncertainty quantification over filtration scale, extending the topological average treatment effect (TATE) analysis of \citet{kim-lee} to conditional mean confidence and individual effect prediction. For the conditional topological average treatment effect (CTATE), we derive multiplier confidence bands at a fixed covariate value, simultaneous over filtration scale, and prove validity in a correctly specified finite-dimensional regression regime, with explicit control of smoothing bias and nuisance-estimation error. For the individual topological treatment effect (ITTE), we integrate existing weighted and functional split-conformal methods to obtain finite-sample marginal prediction coverage under known target-to-calibration likelihood ratios, with a total-variation bound for estimated ratios. We also extend the current TATE silhouette stability analysis to the diagram-independent bound $\|\Phi_r(D)-\Phi_r(D')\|_\infty \le (1+2r)W_1(D,D')$ for $r\geq1$, recovering the known $r=1$ constant, and propagate diagram approximation error to prediction bands. The installable Python library \texttt{tcda\_uq} integrates mean confidence, individual prediction, and topological preprocessing, with tutorials and reproduction materials. Simulations and a PACCE lesion-measurement application illustrate the distinct coverage targets and the importance of declaring the target population.

title: Reliability-Weighted Direct Preference Optimization: Penalized Weights for Robust Preference Learning
abstract: Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) treats every reported comparison as correct, yet preference data contain reversed, tied or otherwise noisy comparisons. RW-DPO gives each comparison an unknown reliability weight $w_i\in[0,1]$ that enters the likelihood linearly -- DPO is $w\equiv1$, a reversed comparison $w_i=0$ -- and estimates the weights jointly with the policy under a minimax-concave penalty on $-\log w_i$. The penalty keeps every comparison the model agrees with at exactly $w_i=1$ and acts only on those it contradicts, through closed-form weight updates at negligible cost over DPO. We prove that recovering all flipped comparisons from a single annotation per comparison requires margins of order $\log n$.
